name: East Ridge and NW Chimney
approach: Start from the Cascade Pass Road trailhead (elevation 3,600 ft). Hike to the base of the CJ Couloir (approximately 0.7 mi). Enter the couloir and ascend to the East Ridge proper. The route then transitions to the NW Chimney section for the final approach to the summit.
descent: From the summit, downclimb/simul-climb back to the top of the technical pitches, then rappel the NW Chimney back down to the moat using gear anchors you build as you go (bring doubles for full-length raps -- there is no fixed hardware on this route). Traverse back to the C-J col and reverse the CJ Couloir (roughly 3,400 ft of downclimbing/rappelling on snow and ice) to the base near the Cascade River, then retrace the short bushwhack and road walk to the trailhead. Avoid the Doug Direct descent some older references mention off the col -- a firsthand trip report calls it a slower, no-safer heather-and-rock traverse than simply reversing the couloir.
hazards: loose, broken rock on the NW Chimney, worse than the published 5.8 grade suggests
rockfall/icefall shedding off Johannesburg's face onto the Sill Glacier just below the couloir
steep snow/ice in the CJ Couloir, especially the last few hundred feet below the col
essentially no fixed protection or rappel anchors on the route
afternoon thunderstorms
early-season stream crossing at the base of the couloir can run high

waysIn.name: Up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to the C-J col
waysIn.season: May-Jun for continuous snow in the couloir
waysIn.notes:
The East Ridge is reached from the Cascade-Johannesburg col, and the direct way there is to climb the couloir that names it. The start is the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft: walk back down the road, drop the embankment into the valley, cross the Cascade River, and go over the moraine onto the couloir apron at roughly 3,300 ft — about twenty minutes from leaving the road. Then roughly 3,400 ft of booting to the col.

This is the fast way and the dangerous way. The couloir carries rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier above, and the snow goes discontinuous where it narrows as the season progresses, so it is an early-season proposition.

The East Ridge by way of the C-J Couloir was first climbed in 1938 and is the most-used line on the peak; it and the other routes finishing on the south side are mostly scrambling.
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier in the couloir
Discontinuous couloir snow after early season
Loose rock and complicated route-finding on the ridge above the col
Existing rappel stations of unknown quality

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The walking way in, avoiding the couloir entirely. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the trailhead at 3,600 ft for 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at roughly 5,400 ft. At the pass, near the benches, turn right and pick up the obvious climbers' path onto Mixup Arm.

Cross Mixup Arm and traverse and descend rightward until you reach the Cache Glacier — the described landmark is a seasonal waterfall, past which you turn right and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

One party using this side reported a long sidehill traverse beneath the Triplets and Cascade Peak, camping in a meadow below the C-J col at about 6,200 ft. That camp puts you at the base of the East Ridge for the following morning without ever entering the couloir.

Early season the traverse across Mixup's flank is snow-covered with a poor runout; late season Cache Col and the glacier edges can moat out.
hazards: Snow-covered traverse on Mixup's flank with bad runout in early season
Cache Col and glacier margins moat out late season
Steep short snow tongue and flanking bergschrunds at Gunsight Notch
Rockfall in the confined ground between snow and rock at the notch
waysIn.whyThisWay: Mid to late season, once the couloir snow breaks up and its rock and ice fall make it too risky; a longer walk and some glacier travel, but it never enters the chute.

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: Approached from the mountain's north side; traverse in below the summit pyramid to reach the low point on the northeast ridge before climbing the ridge itself.
hazards: Snow-filled gullies on the traverse that may require an axe/crampons depending on season

waysIn.name: North-side scree traverse to the ridge crest
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; in early season the north side holds steep snow
waysIn.notes:
Reached from the same Eightmile Lake / Lake Caroline / Windy Pass approach as the West Ridge — Eightmile Lake Trail #1552 for about 2.8 miles to the junction past Little Eightmile Lake, right onto Eightmile-Trout Creek #1554 to Lake Caroline, then on toward Windy Pass and cross-country east onto the west end of the mountain.

Rather than staying on the crest, cross over to the north side of the ridgeline below the summit pyramid and traverse the north-facing scree field eastward.
hazards: Steep north-facing snow with poor run-outs in early season
Loose scree on the traverse
Exposed class 3 if you stay on the crest instead of traversing

name: West Ridge
approach: From the Eightmile Lake Trailhead (~3,300 ft, reached via Icicle Creek Road and Road 7601/Eightmile Road as in the drive note), start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (Trail #1552). The trail climbs through partly burned forest and brushy slopes for about 2.8 miles to a junction just past Little Eightmile Lake (~4,400 ft) — this is the last easy water before the high country. At the junction, branch right (north) onto the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail (Trail #1554), signed toward Lake Caroline. Follow this roughly 2.25–2.75 miles to Lake Caroline, then continue about 0.5 mile to Little Lake Caroline; both lakes sit inside the Enchantments Permit Area, so a permit is required for any overnight camping here. From Little Lake Caroline, continue about 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass (~7,220 ft). Around 6,850 ft, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country to the east, climbing gently; good bivy/camp options appear about 0.5 mile and 250 vertical feet later, around 7,100 ft — this is the last reliable water and the usual high camp for a two-day trip (strong parties push it in a single long car-to-car day, reported at up to ~17 miles round trip). From camp, climb NNE to the broad col on the west side of Cashmere Mountain (~8,000 ft), then follow the west ridge itself up to about 8,200 ft. From there, make a rising traverse/contour several hundred yards around to the northwest side of the summit pyramid to a northwest-facing gully; this gully leads to the summit. The upper ridge is a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by roughly five main notches, and the route weaves back and forth between the north and south sides of the crest rather than following it directly — expect real route-finding, a short snowfield crossing below Windy Pass in early season (an axe/microspikes are worth carrying through mid-summer), and loose, blocky rock with some exposure on the class 3–4 scrambling that begins near the col and continues to the summit.
descent: Descend by reversing the West Ridge exactly as ascended: downclimb the northwest-facing summit gully back to the ~8,200 ft contour, follow the ridge back down through the same notches/gendarmes to the 8,000 ft west col, then drop SSW back to the ~7,100 ft camp/cross-country section and rejoin the Trail #1554/Windy Pass trail. From there retrace the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail past Lake Caroline and Little Eightmile Lake back onto Trail #1552 to the Eightmile Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard West Ridge route; every description of this line treats it as a reversal of the ascent. The class 3–4 sections are the main descent hazard: the ridge's loose, blocky rock and exposed ledges are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend, and it's easy to drift onto the wrong (steeper) side of the crest while trying to retrace the weaving north/south line through the notches — many parties downclimb the steepest short sections (roughly the last 50 ft below each notch) facing in, one at a time. Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the long, open ridge and glissade-able but firm early-season snow near Windy Pass are the other things to plan around; there is no technical descent gear (rope, rack, or anchors) needed for the standard route.
hazards: exposed class 3-4 scrambling on the final ~300 ft summit gully
loose, exfoliating granite on the upper ridge and gully
route-finding through five main gaps on the upper west ridge, switching between the north and south sides of the crest
steep snow in the summit gully into midsummer requiring ice axe/crampons
afternoon thunderstorms
loose talus and scree on the lower approach slopes

waysIn.name: Eightmile Lake to Lake Caroline and Windy Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep once the snowfield below Windy Pass has gone; Jun trips normally still find snow on the traverse
waysIn.notes:
Eightmile Lake Trailhead, reached off Icicle Creek Road and Eightmile Road. Start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (#1552). At about 2.8 miles, just past Little Eightmile Lake, a junction appears — go right onto the Eightmile-Trout Creek Trail (#1554), signed for Lake Caroline.

That trail switchbacks up through a recovering burn. At roughly 5.5 miles it crosses the ridgeline and drops to Lake Caroline, then continues past Little Lake Caroline. From Little Lake Caroline it is about another 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass; Mount Stuart, Dragontail and Colchuck Lake come into view as you gain the pass.

Leave the maintained trail at about 6,850 ft and walk cross-country to the east. Camp spots and the last reliable water appear a little further on, around 7,100 ft. From there climb north-northeast to the broad col on the peak's west side.
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the class 3-4 ground from the col upward
Rockfall onto your own party — the standard advice is to keep the group tight rather than strung out
A snowfield below Windy Pass that persists into mid-summer; an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
A summit block only about the size of a table, with gusts reported over 30 mph

name: Standard Scramble
approach: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Trail tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft, but the bushwhacking through here is described as minimal. From there, stay on the west side of Freezeout Creek, hiking roughly 50-100 ft above the waterline, which gives the most open going through 5,000 ft. At 5,000 ft, cross to the south/east side of the drainage, where the terrain opens into meadow and talus. Above this, climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft. From the notch, the final roughly 700-750 vertical feet to the 8,300+ ft summit is class 2 with short class 3 sections. Total one-way distance from the lakeshore to the summit is on the order of 16-17 miles with close to 7,000 ft of gain from the boat landing alone (the 8,500 ft gain figure reflects the day's cumulative up-and-down, not just net elevation). Freezeout Creek is the reliable water source for essentially the entire approach up to about 5,000-5,500 ft; carry water above that, since there is no dependable source on the upper heather/talus/scree slopes or the summit ridge. Because of the remoteness and boat-access logistics, this is realistically a long single push (18+ hours car-to-car including the taxi) or a one-night backpack, not a casual day hike.
descent: There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb descent that simply reverses the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ground back to the notch on the southwest ridge at ~7,600 ft, then descend the same steep heather/talus/scree slope back into the Freezeout Creek drainage. This is the point where parties get into trouble: the upper basin has several gullies and chutes that look similar from above, and dropping into the wrong one risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek — stick to the exact ascent gully rather than improvising a shortcut. Cross back to the west side of Freezeout Creek at about 5,000 ft, follow the creek down through the old burn, rejoin the Freezeout Creek Trail tread around 4,200 ft, pass back through the cabin at 3,600 ft, and continue down to the abandoned lower Freezeout Creek Trail / Lightning Creek Trail junction, watching again for the flagged diagonal line through the steep rock-and-alder section. Finish on the Lightning Creek Trail back to the Ross Lake shoreline for the return boat/water-taxi pickup. Because of the length of the day, parties commonly finish this descent in the dark (one party that brought its own boat reached the lakeshore around 11:30pm after a roughly 4am start; the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm), so carry headlamps and treat the unmaintained trail sections and creek crossings with extra caution when tired and in low light. Other hazards on the way down include loose, ball-bearing-like scree on the upper slopes (slip/fall risk), the creek crossings themselves if water is high, and afternoon thunderstorm/lightning exposure on the open summit ridge and upper basin — get off the ridge before storms build.
hazards: loose talus
very long approach from the Ross Lake / Hozomeen side or northern Pasayten
abandoned/unmaintained Freezeout Creek Trail with heavy blowdown, notably after the November 2021 flood event
creek crossings (Freezeout Creek) can be high and hazardous in early season
black bear and grizzly bear country - proper food storage required
no cell coverage anywhere on route

waysIn.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
waysIn.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
waysIn.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties with their own boat commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above; the water taxi runs only in the daytime, 8am to 5pm.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
hazards: Abandoned Freezeout Creek trail with heavy blowdown, brush and a hard rock-and-alder diagonal above the junction
Freezeout Creek crossings can be high and hazardous early season
Several similar gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
Loose talus and teetering blocks near the summit; lingering snow patches early season
Boat crossing of Ross Lake with a limited-hours water taxi; long days often finish the descent in the dark
Bear country, no cell coverage, multi-day retreat

waysIn.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
waysIn.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
waysIn.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
hazards: Long unpaved mountain road, steep grades, no passing room, unguarded drop; opens late and closes with early storms
Very long walk in with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary is about a mile north of the summit; crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek
Loose talus and teetering blocks near the summit; lingering snow patches early season
Bear country, no cell coverage, multi-day retreat
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you would rather walk than arrange a boat crossing, and can spare the extra days on foot once the high road to Harts Pass has opened, usually in July.

name: The Drawbridge
approach: The lawful approach is from the US side: cross Ross Lake by boat, follow the Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail, then work round to the glacier below the north face. The first-ascent party instead came in from Canada — from Lightning Lake in Manning Provincial Park, BC, up and over Frosty Mountain, into Princess Creek basin, across the Princess/Crow Creek divide and down into the Crow Creek drainage — but walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing. On that line the first-ascent party camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, about two-thirds of the way down to the approach glacier.
descent: Descend the south side of the peak and the East Ridge back toward camp; the first-ascent party described this walk-off as straightforward ('breezy'), regaining camp near twilight.
hazards: Significant rockfall danger, especially in morning sun
Loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Remote alpine setting with a multi-day approach

waysIn.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
waysIn.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
hazards: Multi-day approach by boat and abandoned, brushy trail; steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the junction
Several unmarked routes on a 1,400 ft wall; identification is by position under the summit only
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall, worst once sun hits the face
Dirt- and moss-filled cracks mid-route and teetering blocks near the top
No cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat

waysIn.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
waysIn.season: Roughly late June through September
waysIn.notes:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
hazards: The described line crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides, one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face; loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Retreat from anywhere on the trip is measured in days
waysIn.whyThisWay: Walks in from the Canadian provincial park over Frosty Mountain, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

waysIn.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass
waysIn.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
hazards: About 27 miles of high walking on the crest to Castle Pass before any off-trail travel
Harts Pass road usually opens only in July
Cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side, then the glacier at the wall's foot
Rockfall on the lower wall and loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Awkward bergschrund or moat; no cell coverage and a multi-day retreat
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you have no boat or water taxi and will walk the roughly 27 miles of crest in, after the Harts Pass road opens, usually in July.

name: La Villa
approach: Same as the Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes (4,859 ft), take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the Pinnacle–Plummer saddle, then contour across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus to the base of Castle's southeast side and scramble up broken ground to reach the base of the summit block. During the Plummer Peak Fire the park closed the Butter Creek Research Natural Area, south of the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the park boundary; its edge runs along the crest at The Castle, so Castle's south side and the east end of this traverse are off limits while that closure stands. Check the park's fire and closure notices before you go.
descent: From the belay ledge atop La Villa, traverse rightward (climber's right) past the true summit to the heavily-trafficked low-5th topout area shared with the Southeast Face route, where fixed slings are typically already in place. Make a single ~40 ft (12 m) rappel back to the base of the technical section, downclimb the 3rd-class terrain below, and reverse the scree traverse and Pinnacle Peak Trail back to Reflection Lakes.
hazards: Exposed scrambling with real fall potential on the approach to the base of the pitch.
Crux slab moves (5.8) well above easier terrain — a fall here has real consequence given the short pitch length and rock ledges below.
Early-season snow/ice on the Pinnacle–Plummer saddle traverse.
Loose rock on the approach scramble and gully
Exposure on the summit block and connecting ridge

waysIn.name: Reflection Lakes and the Pinnacle traverse to the taller summit spire
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The approach is shared with the standard Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes at about 4,859 ft, take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the saddle, then contour east across Pinnacle's south scree to the base of Castle's southeast side, and scramble up broken third-class ground to reach the base of the summit block.

The climbing itself is short: about two-thirds of the pitch is easier ground, there is one solid cam placement, then three slabby crux moves, a jug pull, and easier climbing to a large belay ledge about 10 ft left of the true summit.

From the belay ledge, traverse climber's right past the true summit to the heavily trafficked top-out shared with the Southeast Face, where slings are typically in place, and make a single short rappel back to the base of the technical section.

Stevens Canyon Road typically opens late May and closes with fall snowfall; Narada Falls is the winter and spring trailhead.
hazards: Exposed third-class scrambling with real fall potential just to reach the base of the pitch
A crux high on a short pitch, above ledges
Early-season snow and ice on the traverse from the saddle
Loose rock on the approach scramble and gully
Afternoon thunderstorms and exposure on the summit block and connecting ridge

name: Last Rites
approach: Same Andrews Creek/Chewuch River approach to Cathedral Pass/Upper Cathedral Lake, then toward the Cathedral-Monk gully and along the base to its left, to the open South Face.
descent: From the summit, reverse the Southwest Route. The immediate obstacle is the long chasm that cleaves the summit rocks into north and south sections: you must cross back over it at the 'step-across', stepping onto a chockstone wedged in the slot and mantling a bulge. It is objectively an easy move with enormous exposure, and most parties belay or rig a handline with prusiks for it, especially with a rope, rack and boots on. Below that, downclimb Class 2–3 granite blocks and slabs, following ducks and cairns, and note that a 'cannonhole' further down offers an easier alternative to one vertical step on the ascent line. The angle eases into sandy slopes; drop southwest toward Cathedral Pass (7,600 ft) and pick up the trail for the last 0.6 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake. In early season the chasm can be snow-filled, which makes the first step-across trivial; late season it is bare. Allow 45 minutes camp-to-summit-to-camp on the descent and do not leave it for headlamp time.
hazards: Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured face — helmets on from the base of the wall.
Afternoon convective storms with lightning on an 8,600-ft summit that is the local high point.
Complete absence of cell coverage combined with a 17+ mile trail evacuation makes any injury a multi-day rescue.
Early-season and shoulder-season snow and verglas on the upper face and in the summit chasm.
Wildfire is a recurring late-summer hazard in the Okanogan; smoke and trail closures can shut the approach with little notice.
Black bears are present in the Cathedral Lakes basin; food storage is mandatory in practice.

waysIn.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
waysIn.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
waysIn.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved the whole way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Strong parties walk it in one long day with heavy packs; others split it with a camp partway up the drainage.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.
hazards: Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured face; helmets from the base
Old burn on Andrews Creek: no shade, overgrown wet tread, blowdown
No climbers' trail to the base; identify it by landform
Afternoon storms and lightning on the local high point
Early- and shoulder-season snow and verglas on the upper face and summit chasm
Walk-off crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile trail evacuation; wildfire smoke and closures late summer

waysIn.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
waysIn.season: Roughly mid-July through September
waysIn.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
Trailhead published under several names, one shared with a different trailhead; navigate to the road
No climbers' trail to the base
Rockfall from parties above and loose blocks on the face
Afternoon storms and lightning; snow and verglas on the upper face early or late season
Walk-off crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
No cell coverage and a long trail evacuation
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want the shortest walk and least climbing in, and can accept a drive about two hours longer and 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.

waysIn.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
waysIn.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Long valley approach on the Chewuch trail, longer than Andrews Creek
No climbers' trail to the base; identify it by landform
Rockfall from parties above and loose blocks on the face
Afternoon storms and lightning; snow and verglas on the upper face early or late season
Walk-off crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
No cell coverage and a long trail evacuation
waysIn.whyThisWay: When linking the climb with the Remmel Lake country; a longer walk than the Andrews Creek way, on gentler valley trail.

name: Southeast Buttress
approach: Drive to the Andrews Creek Trailhead (~3,050 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road/FR-51, roughly 22–23.5 miles north of Winthrop. From the trailhead, follow Andrews Creek Trail #504, which climbs steadily through the Andrews Creek drainage — the first ~6-12 miles pass through the 2003 wildfire burn scar, so expect little shade, brushy/overgrown tread in early season (some parties describe being soaked to the skin pushing through wet regrowth after rain), and occasional blowdowns despite periodic trail-crew clearing. Andrews Creek itself parallels the trail for this stretch and is a reliable water source. At about 12 miles the trail tops out at Andrews Pass (6,680+ ft), where the burn gives way to open parkland and meadow with views north toward Amphitheater Mountain; snow patches can linger here into early July. From the pass, continue on the Boundary Trail (#533) through rolling meadows, then take the Cathedral Lakes side trail (bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin) for the final climb to Upper Cathedral Lake — roughly 18 miles and a full, long hiking day from the trailhead. Upper Cathedral Lake is the standard base camp. From camp, cross meadows and talus toward the obvious deep gully separating Cathedral Peak from the smaller pinnacle known as 'The Monk' — this is a 30–60 minute approach. The Southeast Buttress's first pitch starts on the left (north) wall of that gully, a short way in; scramble up onto a tall pedestal that provides a solid belay stance to launch pitch one.
descent: This is a walk-off — there is no established rappel line down the buttress, and multiple independent trip reports (2016, 2018, 2024) confirm parties descend unroped. From the summit, downclimb/scramble west and then southwest along third-class ledges on the peak's west side, aiming to regain the notch/gap system below the true summit block often called the 'summit chasm.' This gap must be crossed (or re-crossed) via an exposed step-across move above a chockstone — rated Class 4 and genuinely no-fall terrain, and the crux of the whole descent; some parties down-lead the last ~15 feet above it and place gear rather than solo it. Once across, continue down loose, blocky slopes and scree southwest, working back around the mountain's west/southwest flank to regain the meadows and talus above Upper Cathedral Lake. Total time from summit back to camp runs about 45 minutes to just over an hour for parties familiar with the line. No rope or rack beyond what's carried for the route itself is needed for a normal, dry descent — several trip reports explicitly note they carried no rappel gear and used none. Do not confuse this descent gully/notch with the SE Buttress ascent line; parties have gotten cliffed out trying to descend the buttress itself, which is why the established walk-off (west then southwest) is strongly preferred. In wet or icy conditions, or for less-experienced parties uneasy with the chasm step-across, building an improvised tree or natural-gear rappel anchor near the notch is a reasonable fallback, but this is not standard practice. The exposed gap crossing near the summit chasm has a walk-around option for parties who'd rather not solo the step-across.
hazards: exposed roped climbing on the buttress
loose sections
long remote northern-Pasayten approach

waysIn.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
waysIn.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
hazards: Long approach through an old burn: little shade, overgrown wet tread
No climbers' trail to the base; navigate by the gully dividing the peak from the tower
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
No-fall step-across on the walk-off descent
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, so retreat is slow
Shorter-looking Canadian approach is an illegal border crossing and patrolled

waysIn.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Trailhead published under several names; long extra drive
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want the shortest walk and least climbing in, and can accept a drive about two hours longer and 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.

waysIn.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
waysIn.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb. The Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road than the Andrews Creek trailhead, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.
hazards: Longest valley approach; trail follows the Chewuch River
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat
waysIn.whyThisWay: When linking the climb with the Remmel Lake country; a longer walk than the Andrews Creek way, on gentler valley trail.

name: Southwest Route
approach: Base at Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft). Shortest way in is the Andrews Creek Trailhead (3,050 ft) at the end of the pavement on FS 51, about 22 miles north of Winthrop: Andrews Creek Trail #504 for roughly 12 miles to Andrews Pass (6,680+ ft), descend into the Spanish Creek drainage about 2 miles to the Spanish Creek Trail junction, then take the Cathedral Lakes trail (just before the cabin, on the right) about 3 miles to the lake — roughly 17 miles and about 4,800 ft of gain. Alternatives: Chewuch River Trail #510 from Thirtymile Trailhead (3,400 ft, 29 miles up FS 51/5160), about 19.9 miles and 4,900 ft of gain on gentle valley trail; and the Boundary Trail #533 from Iron Gate (6,150 ft), about 22 miles to Cathedral Pass. From camp, the climb starts 0.6 trail miles away at Cathedral Pass.
descent: Reverse the route. The step-across is the crux in both directions and is arguably harder going down, since you are stepping onto the chockstone with the exposure in front of you rather than behind; a handline with prusiks is the standard solution and belaying it is entirely reasonable. Lower down, a cannonhole gives an easier alternative to one vertical step you may have climbed on the way up. Below the granite the ground eases into sandy slopes that plunge-step nicely; drop southwest to Cathedral Pass and pick up the trail for the last 0.6 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake. Allow about 45 minutes from summit to camp. If you have descended from a technical route on the south side, you will also traverse a talus fan and drop into the descending gully to rejoin the trail.
hazards: Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across, over easy but committing terrain.
Loose blocks on the Class 2-3 granite outcrops between Cathedral Pass and the summit.
Lightning on the local high point during afternoon convection.
Snow, verglas or fresh snowfall possible in any month at 8,600 ft, which turns the friction moves and the step-across genuinely dangerous.
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile trail evacuation from Upper Cathedral Lake.
Black bears in the basin; heavy mosquitoes near standing water into mid-August.

waysIn.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
waysIn.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
waysIn.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.
hazards: Old burn on the Andrews Creek trail: no shade, brushy tread; a full long day to Upper Cathedral Lake
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending than ascending; second step-across never has snow
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; ducks and cairns are the only markers
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month at 8,600 ft
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin

waysIn.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
waysIn.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek. It is the trail from the high trailhead above Loomis, not the longer Iron Gate route. It walks the least but drives the longest, and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; route marked by ducks and cairns only
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a long evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want the shortest walk and least climbing in, and can accept a much longer drive from Loomis and a climb out at the end.

waysIn.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
waysIn.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb. The valley trail is gentle.

name: Northeast Buttress
approach: Approach as for the Cathedral Pass trail/Southwest Face route via Salmon la Sac and Forest Road 4330 to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, then to Cathedral Pass, from which the Northeast Buttress is reached.
descent: From the summit, work down the south side rather than trying to reverse the buttress. Parties describe slowly picking their way down through a few short fourth-class sections; the south side gets more frequent traffic, which has cleaned much of the loose rock off it compared with the northeast. Follow the Southwest Face line: the Class 2-3 ridge crest southwest, then one or two rappels down the short crux face (a rock horn with fixed slings and rings is the usual anchor — inspect it), then downclimb the main gully and contour back southeast across talus to Cathedral Pass and trail #1345. Retrieve any gear you cached in the trees on the way in. Allow 2-3 hours from the summit back to the pass, plus another 1.5-2 hours down the trail.
hazards: Loose, fractured rock typical of the peak, particularly noted on the variation's second pitch

waysIn.name: Cathedral Rock Trail to the pass, then a rising traverse under the east face
waysIn.season: July to September. The northeast side is shaded and dries slowly, so give it time after rain and expect approach snow into July
waysIn.notes:
From I-90 exit 80 at Cle Elum, take SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake for about 14.8 miles, then gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and the short NF-153 spur to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, Trail #1345, at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit.

The trail climbs through old growth to Nosh Nosh Wahtum, formerly Squaw Lake, at about 4,850 ft and 2.5 miles, then opens into meadow with Cathedral Rock ahead. At about 4 miles you reach Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft and the PCT junction.

Walk north on the PCT for a couple of minutes, then cut across the meadow to a stand of trees. Parties cache the gear they do not need on the climb there. From the trees, start a rising traverse under the east face, past the meadows, and then across a loose talus slope with the northeast buttress in sight.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
hazards: Loose, fractured andesite throughout — poor and unpredictable protection on every technical route on this peak
A short steep snowfield with loose and sharp rock below it, crossed by parties in approach shoes
The moat at the top of the snow
Rockfall down the gully systems from parties, wind and thaw
Descent route-finding on the shattered south and southwest flanks, where many plausible gullies cliff out
Summer convection over the Cascade crest, on an exposed tower with no cell coverage and a remote trailhead

name: Southeast Face Chimney
approach: From I-90 take Exit 80 (Roslyn/Salmon la Sac) about 1 mile west of Cle Elum. Follow Bullfrog Road to the roundabouts, then SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake, roughly 14.8 miles to the end of maintained pavement just past the Salmon la Sac guard station. Continue onto gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and bear slightly left onto the short spur (NF-153) to the Cathedral Rock trailhead (Trail #1345) at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register. The trail climbs steadily through old-growth forest, reaching Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake, ~4,850 ft) at 2.5 miles, then opens into subalpine meadow and blueberry slopes with Cathedral Rock filling the view ahead. At about 4 miles reach Cathedral Pass (5,550 ft) and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Leave the trail at the pass and work up the broken south/southeast slopes and talus toward the base of the tower; the chimney system is on the face directly above, left of the ground taken by the ordinary Southwest Face route. Allow roughly 2.5-3 hours trailhead to Cathedral Pass.
descent: Do not attempt to reverse the chimney. Descend the standard Southwest Face line: from the summit block, scramble the Class 2-3 ridge crest back southwest, then make one or two rappels down the short Class 4+ face section (there is a rock horn near the top of the last pitch with fixed slings and rings that parties routinely use, and a second anchor lower; inspect and back up any tat you find). Below the rappels, downclimb the main gully back to the talus and heather, then pick your way east-southeast to Cathedral Pass and the trail. Route-finding on the descent is the crux for most parties — the broken andesite offers many plausible-looking gullies, most of which cliff out. Note where you came up. Reckon 1.5-2 hours from summit to the pass and another 1.5-2 hours down the trail.
hazards: The intrusive andesite is heavily shattered, giving poor and unpredictable protection quality on all technical routes on the peak.
Rockfall down the gully systems from parties, wind and thaw is the principal objective hazard, and has been repeatedly called out as serious by trip reports.
Route-finding on the shattered south and southwest flanks is genuinely confusing on the descent, and many gullies cliff out above the talus.
Summer convective storms over the central Cascade crest can develop within an hour and put you on an exposed andesite tower.
Residual snow and early-season verglas persist in the shaded chimneys and couloirs into July.
There is no cell coverage and the trailhead is over an hour from the nearest paved highway, so any rescue will be slow.

name: Standard Route (Southwest Face)
approach: Park at the Cathedral Rock Trailhead (elev. ~3,350 ft) at the end of FR-4330 past Salmon La Sac, and start on the signed Cathedral Pass Trail (#1345, Okanogan-Wenatchee NF / Alpine Lakes Wilderness). The trail crosses the Cle Elum River on a footbridge near the start and enters the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary at about 0.5 mile. At roughly 2 miles, stay straight (west) at the Trail Creek Trail (#1332) junction. Squaw Lake, at 2.5 miles, is the last reliable water source and has established campsites if you're splitting the day. Beyond the lake the trail climbs through a subalpine meadow (~3.25 mi) then switchbacks up steeper, rockier tread to Cathedral Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail junction at about 4 miles (5,550 ft) — the end of maintained, signed trail. From the pass, follow the PCT west for less than half a mile to the Peggy's Pond trail junction, then take climbers' boot-paths north toward the peak, either directly up Cathedral Rock's south ridge or via the Peggy's Pond climbers' trail, crossing talus and heather benches to reach the base of the rock's main buttress/gully. Total elevation gain from the trailhead to the base of the technical climbing is roughly 2,700-3,000 ft over 4+ miles of trail, followed by a final few hundred feet of unmaintained, rocky scramble approach. Hazards: loose talus and scree on the off-trail approach, lingering seasonal snow in the entry gully into early summer (can obscure rockfall and require an axe/traction), braided undefined boot-paths near the meadows (stay on durable surfaces — this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness), and rockfall exposure from parties above once you're in the gully/buttress terrain. Stay left of the prominent South Buttress when ascending the scramble gully on the spur. Where the faint path below the base ends, an exposed notch scramble on the right reaches a flat bench; then head left toward the tall spire marking the approach gully, staying left of the gully floor on an exposed ledge to avoid rockfall.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit block back to the ridge crest, then descend the southwest face on the same line used to climb it. At the top of the exposed crux pitch (the awkward-angle pitch most parties rope up for on the way up), the standard descent is one double-rope rappel — parties describe a rock horn near the top rigged with slings and rap rings from prior parties, used as the anchor (natural horn/sling anchor, not bolted). Bring a single 60m rope doubled, or two ropes tied together, to make the ~30m rappel back down onto the SW face/gully; from there, downclimb the loose gully back to the base of the buttress. A minority of parties instead descend via the Northwest Couloir to avoid re-downclimbing the exposed ascent terrain, but that is a variation rather than the standard descent line, and its rappel/anchor situation is not well known — treat it as an alpine-judgment call, not a known bail route. From the base of the rock, retrace the scramble approach back to the Cathedral Pass/PCT junction and follow the maintained Cathedral Rock Trail back to the trailhead. Primary descent hazards are loose rock, very loose everywhere, and rockfall onto parties below — helmets are essentially mandatory, and stagger the group through the gully.
hazards: loose Class 3-4 rock near the summit and throughout the ascent gully
rockfall risk, especially with multiple parties in the gully at once
exposed final moves on the summit block and the crux step below the ridge crest
snow and verglas in the approach/summit gullies into early summer in big-snow years
heavy mosquitoes near Squaw Lake/Cathedral Pass through mid-August

waysIn.name: Cathedral Pass trail #1345 from the Cle Elum River road end
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Oct. Early season, with the gullies still snow-filled, the rockfall hazard is lower — this is the rare Cascade route that is arguably safer under snow
waysIn.notes:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are two trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads north. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading west, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn left, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the left path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.
hazards: Serious rockfall in the summit gully, the peak's named hazard, worst with parties above
Loose rock on the summit scramble as well as in the gully
Picking the Hyas Lake / Deception Pass trailhead by mistake at the road end
Vehicle break-ins at the trailhead
Braided use paths across the meadows near Cathedral Pass

waysIn.name: Peggy's Pond, gaining the summit gully from the ledge above the pond
waysIn.season: Same window; the ledge traverse into the pond is nastier with a heavy pack or under snow
waysIn.notes:
Walk to Cathedral Pass as for the standard, then continue on Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond. The final half mile or so into the pond is primitive, crossing narrow ledges with real exposure, and it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail before it.

Peggy's Pond is the last reliable water and the last established camp, so this is the variant for parties splitting the day or combining the climb with Mount Daniel.
hazards: Exposed narrow ledge traverse on the way into Peggy's Pond
Rockfall in the summit gully
Snow lingering on the pond ledges into early summer
waysIn.whyThisWay: When splitting the trip with a night at the last reliable water, or combining the climb with Mount Daniel; the final ledges into the pond are exposed.

name: North Face
approach: Park at the upper Alpental parking lot (end of Alpental Road, shared with the Snow Lake / Source Lake trailhead). Pick up the maintained Alpental Valley trail, which runs along and above the South Fork Snoqualmie River on the old ski-area service road/cat track for about the first 0.5 mile before narrowing to a standard trail. Continue up-valley roughly 1.5-2 miles, climbing gently through forest and avalanche-path brush with Chair Peak's north side visible ahead; a boot path forks off the main Source Lake/Snow Lake trail toward Source Lake and the basin below Chair Peak's east/north aspect (~4200 ft). From the basin, ascend talus and (in season) a snow apron directly toward the base of the north face at the head of the Alpental cirque, aiming for the obvious snow/ice runnel system below the summit block. Total approach gain to the base is roughly 2,400 ft over about 2.5-3 miles one-way. Hazards: the valley floor and lower slopes cross active avalanche paths below Chair Peak, Snoqualmie Mountain, and The Tooth, so this is a serious slide-prone approach in winter/spring — most parties go early and move quickly through the runout zones; there is also a creek crossing near Source Lake that can be tricky at high flow, and the basin below the face holds a moat late-season that can complicate the final approach to the ice.
descent: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.
hazards: avalanche-prone approach and face
variable winter ice conditions
cornice at the top
short days

waysIn.name: Alpental valley to the Thumb Tack, then over the northeast ridge
waysIn.season: Dec-Mar, below-freezing conditions after a thaw
waysIn.notes: Park at the upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road. Head up the Alpental valley, on the old ski-area cat track for the first stretch and then on trail, toward Source Lake. The maintained tread effectively ends at Source Lake around 3,700-3,740 ft. If stability allows, climb the open slopes at the head of the valley and make a rising traverse into the cirque under Chair's east face, finishing at a freestanding rock called the Thumb Tack. That rock is the one unambiguous fix on the whole approach — use it as your reference, because everything above it is decided by aspect rather than by tread. From the Thumb Tack, go north up a gully to gain the Northeast Ridge. Take the gully rather than attacking the ridge directly from the northeast. This gully is a known avalanche path and has killed climbers. Once on the ridge, follow it to the buttress and round onto the north side of the mountain.
hazards: the gully from the Thumb Tack to the northeast ridge is an avalanche path with a fatal accident history (two deaths in 1996)
avalanche paths cross the approach the length of the Alpental valley
route is only in condition below freezing after a thaw
moat at the base of the face late in the season
creek crossing near Source Lake at high flow

name: Northeast Buttress
approach: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Hazards: the basin and approach gully sit below avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain — this is a classic early-season slide path, and parties often describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity, and wind-loaded slopes here; a rope/axe/crampons are typically carried from the basin onward given the exposure of the approach gully itself.
descent:
From the top of the buttress, scramble back across the flat summit area and drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the gully further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down it and take the very first left it offers, and the rappel station comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

The station is fixed and old — three rusty pitons tied together with a mass of aging webbing and a pair of aluminium rappel rings. Two ropes give a single 60 m rappel that clears the corniced lip and lands where the gully opens out and ends; a single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully exposed to whatever comes down the gully. Move to the side of the gully mouth once you are down so the next person cannot drop anything on you. A tag line is worth carrying for exactly that reason — it buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in the fall line.

A second gully further along is an alternative rather than a continuation: it carries both an upper and a lower anchor, so a single rope is enough to get through that one instead. Anchors on this descent are not maintained and may not be where you want them — carry cord and a knife to re-rig, and expect that getting around remaining steep snow at the base may take an extra downclimb or rappel.

Below the rappel, plunge-step or downclimb 35-40° snow to the base of the east face and traverse east to rejoin the approach. Cornice collapse at the gully lip, sloughing in warm conditions, and rock knocked down by parties above are the main descent hazards.

Rappelling the buttress itself is a documented summer alternative, taking four to five shorter rappels off a tree, a second gnarlier tree, an old pair of bolts and a rock horn.
hazards: rockfall
variable rock quality
winter avalanche terrain

waysIn.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct, snow-free
waysIn.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply right from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the north side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet
waysIn.whyThisWay: Summer and fall, once the snow is gone and the buttress is climbed as a rock route; the basin path avoids the early-season slide gully.

waysIn.name: Winter and spring, on snow
waysIn.season: Dec-Apr, ice and mixed
waysIn.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below

name: Voie de Chaise
approach: From the Alpental parking lot, follow the standard summer trail toward Source Lake and the East Face approach, crossing talus fields and a snow patch, then a final stretch of loose scree to the base of the route; about 2-3 hours from the parking lot.
descent: Most parties rappel the route on a single 60 m rope, using two rappel stations added in 2023. Belay the leader back down pitch 8 rather than rappelling it: rappelling it knocks loose rock onto anyone below. From the top anchor, rappel straight down to the chain anchor just right of the pitch-6 belay, then to the top of pitch 5, then down the belay stations to the ground, seven rappels in all. Several leave less than 5 ft of rope to spare, so knot the ends. If other parties are on the route, descend the East Gully instead: hike, downclimb and rappel the normal descent.
hazards: Loose rock sections higher on the route
Tight rappel-rope margins requiring careful rope management

waysIn.name: Alpental and the Source Lake talus to the Chair snow patch, then the east face scree
waysIn.season: Summer into autumn, once the snow patch below the face has shrunk and the rock is dry
waysIn.notes: From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, take the summer trail toward Source Lake. Where the trail meets the talus field, do NOT drop down — dropping is the turn for The Tooth. Instead hold your height and gain 100 to 200 horizontal feet until you can pass small cliff bands on your right. Above them the tread improves and runs just below a waterfall. Leave the trail at a longer talus field, usually marked by a large cairn, and climb up and left on good paths between the talus to the permanent snow patch under the east face. Climb the snow patch to its top, then take the last 200 to 300 ft of loose scree, keeping hard against the base of the peak where the scree lies at a gentler angle. Reckon two to three hours from the car to the foot of the route.
hazards: The final 200-300 ft of approach scree is loose and sits directly under the face
A newer alpine line: loose pebbles and small rock still come off the upper pitches, and the last two pitches were left very dirty after cleaning
Several rappels leave under 5 ft of rope to spare on a 60m — knots in the ends are not optional
The eighth pitch must be belayed back down rather than rappelled, because rappelling it showers rock on anyone below
Parties stacked on the face: this and the East Face share the same descent gully

name: West Ridge
approach: From the Alpental lot, follow the standard Northeast Buttress approach to the base of that buttress, then keep traversing west beneath the north face on slabby terrain that can be snowy and glide-cracked in early season to reach the base of the route, roughly 2-2.5 hours from the parking area.
descent: From the summit, descend via the standard south-side couloir, which funnels into the same narrow rappel gully used by the other Chair Peak routes; reported descent time is about 1-2 hours back to the Chair Peak basin.
hazards: Loose rock in sections of the ridge
Limited protection on specific short sections
Early-season snow/glide-crack hazard on the approach

waysIn.name: Alpental and the Northeast Buttress approach, then round onto the slabs on the west side
waysIn.season: Spring into mid-summer while the slabs still hold snow that can be crossed; a light axe and light crampons are the usual kit until midsummer, after which it goes on dry rock
waysIn.notes:
Use the standard Chair Peak trailhead at Alpental, the same start the Northeast Buttress uses. From the basin, traverse slabby ground round onto the west side of the peak. Early in the season that slab traverse holds snow and can be cut by glide cracks, which is the part of this approach worth respecting rather than the walking.

Roughly two to two and a half hours from the parking area to the foot of the route.
hazards: Early-season snow on the slab traverse, with glide cracks opening in it
Loose rock along the ridge crest
Sections of the crest with little available protection
The descent couloir on the south side funnels into the same narrow rappel gully every other Chair Peak route uses, so expect traffic above you

name: Southeast Slopes
approach: Two established approaches reach the southeast-side gullies, and both are worth knowing since parties come at this route from either direction. (1) PCT from Snoqualmie Pass: From the PCT North Trailhead (Trail #2000) off Exit 52, the trail switchbacks up through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and hits the exposed rock-cut traverse of Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 (~5,400 ft) — a good checkpoint, though don't count on water here late season. Continue north past Ridge Lake (~mile 6.5, reliable camping and water) and the Alaska Lake/Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling, rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry–Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face; note the Park Lakes Trail junction here, which ties in the Mineral Creek approach below. At roughly mile 13.5 — about a half-mile short of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp where the trail dips to about 5,500 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy/heather slopes into the gully systems on the south/southeast face. Do not continue on to Chikamin Pass itself before cutting uphill: doing so puts you in the middle of the Four Brothers, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain. One-way distance from the trailhead to the base of the gullies is about 13.5 miles with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp along the PCT (Ridge Lake or the pack camp near the turnoff) and treat this as a 2–3 day trip rather than a car-to-car push. (2) Mineral Creek/Park Lakes approach: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331) at the end of FR-46/Cooper Pass Road (~2,400 ft), the trail is brushy lower down but well-trodden; it climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes (~4.3–5.4 mi, ~2,570 ft gain) and ties into the PCT. From the PCT/Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above the lake — parties describe brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down, with some exposure near the final ridge crest. This is the shortest line in (day-trip feasible for strong parties, roughly 14–16.5 mi round trip) but involves rougher tread and creek crossings lower on the trail. Either way, once above treeline the gully system itself is loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in its upper sections — expect Class 2 hiking low, stepping up to sustained Class 3 (with a short, well-protected Class 4 chimney/slot right below the summit block on some lines) as you gain Chikamin Ridge and approach the summit horn.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb route — no rappelling on the standard line. From the summit, reverse the ascent gully: downclimb the short crux chimney/slot below the summit block (Class 3, with one low-Class-4 move reported on some lines), then work back down the heather benches and slabs to the broad gully on the south side of Chikamin Ridge. Descend the gully itself carefully — it is loose scree and dirt underfoot, with real rockfall potential onto anyone below, so keep the group tight and go one at a time through the narrower sections — back down to the grassy slopes above the PCT. Rejoin the trail either near the pack camp at the turnoff (if you came up via Snoqualmie Pass/PCT) or continue down past Glacier Lake toward the Park Lakes/Mineral Creek trail (if using that approach), matching whichever line you climbed. Some parties have improvised alternate descents off the east ridge or down toward Chikamin Lake to the northeast; at least one party describes that variation as loose, unprotected Class 4 downclimbing requiring a hand-line/'panic rope' for security through a 6,600 ft notch — that is an exploratory off-route line, not the standard descent, and shouldn't be treated as such. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are reported anywhere on this route. A short hand-line for the summit-block chimney is a reasonable optional safety margin for less confident scramblers, but it is not a technical rappel, and 0 rappels are needed on the standard route.
hazards: loose scree
rockfall
long trail approach
unmarked gully turnoff near Chikamin Pass — easy to wander into the cliffy "Four Brothers" towers
steep, snow-filled gully in early season can be a rubble-choked chute
short but exposed Class 3 moves on the summit horn

waysIn.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile short of Chikamin Pass
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the pack camp near the turnoff and make it a two or three day trip.
hazards: Long trail approach (about 13.5 miles one way) with camps well short of the peak
Unmarked gully turnoff half a mile short of Chikamin Pass; overshooting puts you among the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
Steep snow-filled, rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed Class 3 moves on the summit horn
waysIn.whyThisWay: On a two- or three-day trip camping along the Pacific Crest Trail, taking about 24 miles round trip for the scenery instead of the shorter, rough and brushy Mineral Creek tread.

waysIn.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach, no maintained tread
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies above Glacier Lake
Snow-filled gullies in early season
Exposure near the final ridge crest; short exposed Class 3 moves on the summit horn

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Graves Creek Trailhead in the SW corner of Olympic National Park, follow the East Fork Quinault River Trail (Enchanted Valley Trail) east. The first roughly 2 miles follow an old roadbed through big firs and cedar before a short, steep drop to river level; at 2.5 miles the trail crosses Pony Bridge, a narrow, photogenic span over a fern-lined gorge — a reliable early water source before the long valley slog. From there the trail undulates through old-growth rainforest (spruce, alder, maple) to O'Neil Creek Camp at about mile 6.7, then crosses No Name Creek and Pyrites Creek around miles 8–9.5 (Pyrites has camps on both banks, ~12 sites total, and is a good staging point for a two-day approach). Beyond Pyrites the trail climbs gently for several more miles, including a high bridge roughly 20 ft above the river that can feel exposed if snow-covered early season. Around mile 13 the trail opens into Enchanted Valley (~2,000 ft) at the historic chalet, directly beneath Chimney Peak's southeast face, which rears 4,800 ft above the valley floor in under a mile — far too steep and cliff-bound for the standard route.
