From the valley (climbers appear to peel off the maintained trail somewhat short of the chalet, roughly mid-valley), leave the trail and work cross-country around the mountain's south/southwest flank — brushy, unmarked, boulder-and-timber route-finding with no cairns — up a drainage that gains the SW ridge crest, where the Class 3 scrambling begins. Given the 13-mile one-way trail approach, most parties camp in the valley (Pyrites Creek or Enchanted Valley) and climb the peak as a long day from camp rather than car-to-car.
descent: Descend by reversing the SW ridge scramble line back toward the valley — the same Class 3 terrain used on ascent — since the peak's cliff-girt southeast and north aspects offer no easier walk-off. Downclimbing is straightforward for a competent scrambling party, but loose rock and fast-forming cloud (the Olympics sock in quickly) make route-finding the main hazard; stay well back from the southeast face's edge, which drops 4,800 ft to Enchanted Valley in under a mile. Parties less comfortable reversing the short exposed step(s) low on the ridge sometimes opt for one short, single-rope rappel off a natural anchor (sling around a horn or block — no fixed bolts or chains are documented for this route) rather than downclimb it; a single 30–60m rope is more than sufficient. Treat this as an optional, situational rappel rather than a mandatory one — many parties downclimb the whole ridge. Once back to valley-floor terrain, work cross-country back to the Enchanted Valley Trail and reverse the ~13-mile trail hike to Graves Creek Trailhead, re-crossing Pyrites Creek, No Name Creek, and Pony Bridge.
hazards: very remote central-Olympics location
Class 3-4 rock with exposure near the summit
loose rock

name: South Peak via East Gully
approach: This route shares the same trailhead-to-basin approach as the East Face: from the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616, hike the Pete Lake Trail #1323 (~4 easy miles to Pete Lake, then ~2 more miles) to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, head north on the PCT about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche-path crossing, then leave the PCT and follow the climber's path (flagged/cairned, fords Chimney Creek and crosses several brushy ravines) up through Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft, ~4-5 hrs from the trailhead) to the moraine and the bivy basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier (~5,400 ft) — see the East Face route's approach text for full turn-by-turn detail on this shared stretch, and treat it as a 2-3 day car-to-car trip. Above camp, a wet, grubby gully through the rock band leads onto the upper Chimney Glacier; rope up, cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, and be ready to improvise around the moat at the foot of the rock, which gets worse later in the season. Water and camping options match the East Face approach: Pete Lake, the low Chimney Creek crossings, or melted glacier snow above the moraine.
descent: Descend the line of ascent. From the South Peak, return about 400 ft to the notch between the central and south summits, then follow the ledge system back down; the ledges are easy to pick out from above. Rappel the steeper, wet fourth-class steps on a single 60 m rope rather than downclimbing them. No fixed anchors are known on this line, so carry slings, cord and a few rap rings to build and leave your own. Cross the moat back onto the glacier, reverse the glacier and the gully through the rock band, and return to camp.
hazards: rockfall
crevasses on the approach glacier
exposed summit pitch
long approach

waysIn.name: Chimney Glacier to the East Gully
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Shares the whole trailhead-to-basin stretch with the East Face line: the Pete Lake Trail to the lake, on to the Pacific Crest Trail, north about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche path, then a flagged climbers' path on the east bank of Chimney Creek up through steep brush and several ravines to Sunrise Knob at about 4,650 ft and the bivy basin at the toe of the glacier. Budget four to five hours car to knob and treat the whole outing as two or three days. Above camp, climb the moraine and take the wet, grubby gully through the rock band onto the ice, then rope up and cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits.
hazards: Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier
A moat at the base of the face that widens badly through late season
Rock that stays wet on this aspect, so short fourth-class steps feel harder than their grade
Rockfall out of the gullies above the glacier
Long, remote approach with no quick retreat

name: Southwest Route / Standard
approach: Park at Trinity Trailhead (~2,800 ft), at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old Trinity mine site. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 up the valley; at roughly 1.4–1.5 miles, bear right (northeast) at the junction onto the Chiwawa River Trail #1550, an old mining-road grade that continues up-valley along the river (reliable water the whole way here). Follow the Chiwawa River Trail about 3.7 more miles to the signed Red Mountain Trail junction at Chiwawa Mountain's southeastern foot — roughly 5 miles and the last easy, obvious water before the basin. Most parties bear left here into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain. The tread beyond the junction is rougher and sometimes braided; it climbs about a mile-plus through forest and then subalpine meadow toward the ~5,500 ft basin below the Fortress-Chiwawa col. Expect a shallow ford of the Chiwawa River/headwater creek in this stretch, and favor the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin to avoid brush-whacking. Above the basin, gain the ~6,300 ft bench via talus/scree gullies or vegetated slopes just left of them — early-season parties will find snow gullies here (ice axe/crampons recommended) that are faster than the loose summer scree. From the bench, the standard finish is a class 2 scramble up slabs and gullies on the southwest face; the short section gaining the summit ridge is the route's crux — loose, exposed class 2–3 rock — after which an easy ~100 ft rightward (west) traverse leads to the summit. One-way distance from Trinity is roughly 7–8 miles with about 5,700 ft of gain; most parties camp in Chiwawa Basin or on the 6,300 ft bench and treat it as an overnight, though fit parties do it car-to-car in a long day. A less-traveled alternate approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead, bushwhacking to about 5,500 ft and following a gully right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then easy Class 2 along the west ridge.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the southwest scree/gully slopes to the 6,300 ft bench, staying off the looser climber's-left skyline gully in favor of the main descent gullies/vegetated slopes used on the way up. Continue down into Chiwawa Basin, re-ford the creek, and retrace the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and Buck Creek Trail #1513 back to the Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling anywhere on it — none is typically required. Watch for loose rock and scree underfoot on the upper southwest slopes (a common complaint on nearby Fortress Mountain's gullies applies here too), and in early season the same gullies used for the ascent can be glissaded or skied for a much faster descent when snow-covered.
hazards: loose rock/talus on the west ridge and upper mountain
early-season snow and cornices near the Fortress-Chiwawa col
misidentifying the correct gully near the col — the wrong line leads to an exposed low-5th-class dead end
long remote approach with no reliable cell coverage

waysIn.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
waysIn.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
waysIn.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and bear right at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear left into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 under storm-damage order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is not reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also closes the Chiwawa River Road and the trails from Trinity through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 (order 06-17-07-2026-11, through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is unreachable by vehicle

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
waysIn.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
waysIn.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you prefer the shorter line on paper from Phelps Creek and can handle a trail-less bushwhack with no good camp; for parties who know the area.

name: Chockstone Route
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft) on SR-20, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, and locate the obvious chasm/gully between North and South Early Winters Spire on the west side of the formations. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base; expect to switch between rock shoes and boots/crampons if snow lingers in the gully.
descent: The standard descent uses four bolted rappel stations with a 60m rope, plus one rappel off a tree down the 5.0 slab near the start, located about 30m down and skier's-right of the summit exit. An older/original variant instead makes five rappels straight down the ascent gully, including one free-hanging rappel off the chockstone, through loose and windy terrain; this is considered slower and less pleasant than the bolted West Face option.
hazards: Much loose rock on the upper pitches, which are often simul-climbed — rockfall risk to your own party and anyone below
Lingering snow/ice in the gully into early summer; a cold, wet crux pitch has been reported to climb closer to 5.8+

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail to the chasm between the two spires
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream and a large cairn, then take the climbers' path up through slabs, talus and heather into the basin below the west faces.

The objective from here is the huge cleft that splits the two Early Winters Spires, seen from the west side. Head for its foot. Note this is the west-side gully — the couloir that splits the same two spires on the east side, reached from the highway hairpin, is a different feature and a different route.

Be ready to swap between rock shoes and boots if snow is still lying in the gully.
hazards: snow lingering in the gully early season — axe and crampons
loose rock funnelled down the gully, including from parties above
wind in the gully; it channels weather

name: Walrus Glacier
approach: Start at the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, end of White River Road/FR-6400). Follow White River Trail #1507 south along the flat valley floor for about 4 miles - easy grade but notoriously buggy/mosquito-heavy in early-to-mid summer - to its junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562. Turn onto Boulder Creek Trail and climb roughly 4.5 miles through forest into Boulder Creek Basin, fording Boulder Creek (unbridged) around 4,000 ft; in early season this crossing is cold and knee-to-thigh deep and sometimes braids into two or three separate channels. Established camps sit in the open basin between about 4,900 and 5,300 ft (roughly 8.5 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the car), and given the scale of this outing (~22-23 miles round trip, 6,200-6,500+ ft one-way gain to the summit) most parties treat this as a base camp rather than a car-to-car day. From camp, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather/talus north toward Boulder Pass (~6,300 ft) - a direct fall-line push from about 5,800 ft takes roughly 1.5 hours. Two lines diverge from the pass area: for the glacier line, go down steep snow on the far side of the pass and climb to a bench near 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm, and rope up there for crevassed glacier travel (crampons and axe required); then traverse east across the basin under Peak 7242, crossing its NE ridge near 6,700 ft, then turn west (~30 min) to reach the toe of the Walrus Glacier (marked 'Clark Glacier' on some maps). For the non-glacier south-basin alternative, stay climber's-left, gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, and locate the single easy gully near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band; contour broken rock and lingering snow to the final south/west ridge and a short class 3 scramble to the summit. Water is reliable along the White River and in Boulder Creek Basin but essentially absent above camp - fill up before the push. Key hazards: the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, heavy mosquitoes on the valley approach, wet-slide/avalanche-prone slopes on the basin traverse into early summer, and genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin - parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.
descent: Reverse the ascent line back to Boulder Creek Basin camp, then out via Boulder Creek Trail #1562 and White River Trail #1507 to the trailhead. If you climbed via the Walrus Glacier, descend the same glacier line back down to the 6,700 ft bench and over Boulder Pass, staying roped through the crevassed sections and unroping once back on stable moraine/talus below the ice. If you climbed/are descending the non-glacier south-basin alternative, downclimb the same class 3-4 gully and ridge terrain you ascended back to the heather slopes above camp. Watch for lingering wet-snow avalanche debris on the basin traverse below Boulder Pass in early/mid-summer, and re-ford Boulder Creek on the way out. This is fundamentally a long walk-off/scramble descent, not a rappel-dependent one.
hazards: Walrus Glacier crevasses
loose summit rock
long approach

waysIn.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
waysIn.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late in the season, or when you have no glacier gear, once the crevasses on the glacier have opened up; a walk-up line from the same basin.

waysIn.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
waysIn.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
waysIn.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

The bench is where you rope up. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here

name: Classic Route
approach: Start at the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road (~1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes, elev. ~4,500 ft). Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail about 1.25 miles, with roughly 350 ft of up-and-down, to Snow Lake at ~4,600 ft — the last reliable water source. Skirt the west/north shore of the lake; the maintained tread continues a short way over a tree-covered rise before petering out into talus. From there work up and right toward an obvious talus/dirt gully on the peak's NW side — a climbers' path picks up again on a heather bench near the top of the gully. Follow this into the basin below Unicorn Peak, ascending moraine along the left (south) side of the small permanent snow patch/glacier remnant in the basin (crampons/an axe are handy in early season on the couloir above, though not strictly required most of the year). A climbers' path traverses below the cliffs here, offering easier travel than the loose scree and talus on either side, and leads up to the saddle (Unicorn Col) just west of the summit. From the saddle, a use trail traverses east/around the south side of the main summit block, across a final loose scree slope, to the base of the summit horn. Total approach is roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft of gain; expect route-finding through talus and some loose rock once off the maintained trail, and possible steep snow in the gully/basin into mid-summer.
descent: Downclimb or rappel back down the same south-face line you climbed. The rappel anchor is a large rock horn on the south side of the summit block (a bleached/dead tree or snag was used historically — that anchor is no longer sound and should not be trusted; use the rock horn, which parties describe as backed with slings/webbing and sometimes rappel rings). This is a single-rope rappel of roughly 40-50 ft down the pinnacle's south face; a 30m rope is generally described as enough to both lead the route and make the rappel, though at least one party found a 30m rope fell just short and recommended a 37-40m rope to be safe, and notes there are effectively two rappel options from the top — one drops directly to the notch/ground below the horn, the other lands you on the glacier/snow patch side, so confirm which station you're using and its exact length before committing. After the rappel (or downclimb, which is a viable option for confident 4th/low-5th-class scramblers but notably exposed), reverse the approach: back across the scree slope and around to the saddle, down through the basin and gully to Snow Lake, then out the Snow Lake Trail to the trailhead.
hazards: Loose blocks reported occasionally on the approach scramble to the base

waysIn.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the middle line on the summit horn
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Shared approach with the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, take the maintained Snow Lake Trail about a mile and a quarter and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last water. Skirt the west and north shore; the tread continues a short way over a tree-covered rise before petering out into talus.

Work up and right toward the obvious talus and dirt gully on the peak's northwest side; a climbers' path picks up again on a heather bench near the top of the gully. Follow it into the basin, then climb moraine along the left side of the small permanent snow patch to Unicorn Col just west of the summit. A climbers' path traverses below the cliffs — easier travel than the scree either side — and leads east around the south side to the base of the summit horn.

The climb itself is a single pitch of blocky low-fifth-class climbing, about 40-50 ft, on the south and southeast face, with one fixed piton mid-pitch.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.
hazards: Loose blocks on the approach scramble to the base of the horn
A short exposed pitch above broken ground where a fall has real consequence
A rappel that may not reach the ground on a 30 m rope, particularly with an open moat late season
An old bleached snag at the top that is no longer a sound anchor
Two different rappel lines off the same block landing in different places

name: Classic Route
approach: Start from the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road (open roughly Memorial Day through mid-October) or, when the road is gated by snow, from the Narada Falls pullout — from Narada Falls a short, steep ~200 ft climb through open timber gets you up to Stevens Canyon Road. From either start, walk the road roughly half a mile to the point where it bends sharply and begins heading east; leave the pavement here and drop south through sparse, open forest toward Tatoosh Creek, losing a couple hundred feet to reach it around 4,500 ft. Cross the creek (a rock-hop most of the season, more involved during peak snowmelt) and angle up onto a broad talus slope — about 250 vertical feet — that runs down to the creek (snow-covered in spring, boulder-hopping by mid/late summer). At the top of the talus, continue up through trees staying right of a short cliff band (the timber here is brushy and it's easy to drift toward the cliff if you're not paying attention). Roughly 700 ft above the creek crossing (~5,200 ft) you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue up to the broad 5,440 ft saddle between Lane Peak and Denman Peak. From the saddle, turn right (west) and climb moderate open ground aiming for the obvious gully weakness in the southeast face — this is the 'prominent gully' the route is named for. Follow it up, trending left near the top for the final short scramble (mostly Class 3 with plentiful holds, plus a few exposed 4th-class moves) to the 6,012 ft summit. Round trip from the road is a bit over 3 miles with roughly 1,400-1,500 ft of gain; there is no reliable water past Tatoosh Creek. Hazards: spring snow/avalanche debris and wet rock in the creek drainage and talus, brushy route-finding through the timber band, and loose rock / rockfall exposure in the summit gully, especially with parties above.
descent: This is mostly a downclimb; the sturdy tree in the gully allows an optional rappel over the loosest section. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the summit scramble and the southeast-face gully back to the 5,440 ft Lane–Denman saddle, then drop east back through the timber (staying right of the cliff band on the way down, mirroring the ascent line) to the top of the talus slope. Descend the talus to Tatoosh Creek, re-cross, and climb back up to Stevens Canyon Road, then walk back to the Narada Falls or Reflection Lake pullout. Watch for loose rock and inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully (plunge-stepping is fine on consolidated snow but the gully holds loose rock once it melts out), and take care not to cliff yourself out in the timber band by drifting off the ascent line.
hazards: loose rock and rockfall potential in the narrow summit gully
exposed 4th-class moves just below the true summit
Tatoosh Creek crossing at ~4,500 ft can be difficult during high spring runoff
afternoon thunderstorms are common over the Tatoosh Range in summer

waysIn.name: Tatoosh Creek, the timber band and the Lane-Denman saddle
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start from the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road, open roughly late May through mid-October, or from Narada Falls when the road is gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber gains the road.

Walk the road roughly half a mile to where it bends sharply and begins heading east. Leave the pavement there and drop south through sparse open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft, losing a couple of hundred feet. Cross the creek — a rock-hop most of the season, more involved at peak snowmelt — and angle up a broad talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.

At the top of the talus, continue up through trees staying right of a short cliff band. Roughly 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft, you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue to the broad Lane-Denman saddle at about 5,440 ft.

From the saddle, turn right and climb moderate open ground to the gully weakness in the southeast face. Follow it up, trending left near the top for a final short scramble to the summit. Round trip is a bit over 3 miles with roughly 1,400-1,500 ft of gain, and no water past Tatoosh Creek.
hazards: Cliffing out in the brushy timber band if the line drifts left of the cliff band
Loose rock and rockfall in the narrow summit gully, especially with parties above
Exposed fourth-class moves just below the true summit
Tatoosh Creek can be difficult during high spring runoff
Afternoon thunderstorms are common over this range in summer
Inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully once it melts out

name: Clean Break
approach: Park at the pullout where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek near milepost 171, about 8.5 miles east of Washington Pass. A good climbers' trail follows the east side of the creek for a couple of miles, then crosses it and climbs talus and forest up the western edge of the valley toward Juno Tower; at about 5,000 ft a rising traverse leftward threads most of the slide alder to the foot of the east prow. The usual way down is the Burgundy Col trail to the Wine Spires pullout near milepost 166, farther west on the highway: from Burgundy Col (~7,720 ft) it drops to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (good camping and a late-season spring near 6,400-6,500 ft), descends the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft) past a trail register, and climbs a short loose talus/scree slope back up to the road. Walking up the east side of Silver Star Creek from the pullout is mostly simple open cross-country to the base, with little bushwhacking if you pick your line.
descent: Two descent options exist: (1) From the summit, traverse south toward Bench Camp below Burgundy Col; this takes approximately 1 hour to reach Bench Camp. From Bench Camp, follow the established trail down to Highway 20 (approximately 1 hour more), then hitch-hike back to the vehicle. (2) Alternatively, scramble northwest to Sunset Col and descend the Sunset Col trail back toward Silver Star Creek drainage, rejoining the approach route.
hazards: Pitch 1 requires solid protection skills in splitter crack
Upper portions expose climbers to rockfall
Approach crosses significant talus requiring care
Afternoon thunderstorms common mid-summer

waysIn.name: Silver Star Creek to the east prow of Juno Tower
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Clean Break faces east, and the direct line to it is the Silver Star Creek drainage rather than the Burgundy Creek path used for the Wine Spires. Park at the small pullout on SR-20 roughly eight and a half miles east of Washington Pass. A good climbers' trail follows the east side of the creek for a couple of miles, then crosses the creek and climbs talus and forest up the western edge of the valley toward the foot of Juno Tower. At about 5,000 ft, make a rising traverse leftward across the slope; taken at the right height this threads most of the slide alder and lands you under the tower's east prow. Parties reverse this on descent, or cross west and drop back to the highway on the standard Burgundy Col trail.
hazards: Slide alder on the rising traverse below the wall
Rockfall onto the lower pitches from parties above
Fifteen pitches with the crux in the first hundred feet — a committing day once started
Afternoon storms on an exposed east prow

name: Southwest Slopes
approach: The standard approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft), at the end of Forest Road 6211 off the Chiwawa River Road (FR 62) north of Leavenworth. From the trailhead, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the valley along Phelps Creek, gaining about 1,900 ft over 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows; you enter the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary around the 2.5-mile mark, and Phelps Creek itself is the reliable water source the whole way up (a couple of minor tributary crossings, easy on foot/log in normal summer flow). Beyond the meadows the trail climbs into upper Phelps Basin toward the base of Spider Glacier at roughly 5,300 ft, then ascends the glacier/snowfield about 0.5 mile to Spider Gap (7,100 ft) — this is the crux of the approach: it's a permanent snow/glacier slope that is generally a straightforward boot-pack or plunge-step in summer but can have open crevasses and firm, icy conditions early season, so carry (and know how to use) an ice axe, and microspikes are a common recommendation; whiteout or early-morning refreeze can make an axe/crampons more than optional. From Spider Gap descend the north side — about 100 vertical feet of the steepest snow (softer, less sun-affected snow tends to be climber's-left/north), then scree, then an easing snowfield — down roughly 3.5 miles past the Lyman Glacier and Upper Lyman Lakes to Lower Lyman Lake (~5,587 ft). From Lower Lyman Lake, climb back up through open meadows for about 1.8 miles to Cloudy Pass (~6,438 ft), the normal camp/staging point for the peak. From Cloudy Pass, Cloudy Peak's summit is well under a mile away and about 1,500 ft higher: an obvious boot path leads up through wildflower meadows onto rocky talus, gaining the peak's southwest ridge. Follow the ridge crest itself — straying off it onto the flanking slopes drops you into seriously unstable scree/talus — picking a careful line through loose talus blocks to avoid kicking rock onto anyone below; the ridge has real exposure with a precipitous drop on its far (north) side. At the base of the final summit block, traverse around to its east side and then work around toward the north (back) side to find a walkable weakness through the Class 4+ short scramble to the true summit; this last bit is narrow with real exposure and is the route's technical crux. Three approaches reach Cloudy Pass: besides the line described here, Cloudy Pass/Cloudy Peak can also be reached via the Buck Creek Trail #1513 from the Trinity Trailhead over Buck Creek Pass, or via the Railroad Creek Trail from Holden Village (reached by Lake Chelan boat/vehicle shuttle) past Lower Lyman Lake — both longer, multi-day alternatives to the Phelps Creek/Spider Gap line described above, which is the one the Leavenworth/US-2 road drive serves.
descent: Descent is a walk-off/downclimb by the same southwest-ridge route — there is no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Reverse the short Class 4+ summit-block scramble (west/back around to the east side, one hand on rock, mind the narrow, exposed step), then follow the southwest ridge crest back down, staying directly on the ridge rather than cutting onto the flanking scree, which is notably looser and harder to descend safely; loose talus underfoot means slower, deliberate footwork rather than a technical hazard. Trip-report accounts describe the descent as straightforward 'easier hiking downhill' once off the summit block, using the distant camp at Cloudy Pass as a natural navigation reference back down through the talus and meadows to camp — figure roughly the same time or somewhat less than the ascent for this short (under a mile, ~1,500 ft) summit push. From Cloudy Pass, retrace the approach: down through meadows to Lower Lyman Lake, back up and over Spider Gap (descending its snow/scree slope requires the same caution — and ice axe if carried — as the ascent, since it's the steepest, most exposure-sensitive terrain of the whole car-to-car trip), then down Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to the Phelps Creek Trailhead. Parties camping at Cloudy Pass or Upper Lyman Lakes rather than doing the whole thing car-to-car in a day will simply reverse the relevant leg back to camp before continuing out the following day.
hazards: loose scree
snow on slopes early season
exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with a steep drop-off — many parties stop below the true summit
shifting/unstable talus off the main ridgeline

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek and Spider Gap (standard)
waysIn.season: Jul–Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft), Trail #1511 climbs the valley about 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows, then into upper Phelps Basin and up the Spider Glacier snowfield to Spider Gap at 7,100 ft. Descend the north side — the steepest 100 vertical feet first, softer snow tends to be climber's-left — then scree and easing snowfield past the Lyman Glacier to Lower Lyman Lake, and back up about 1.8 miles of open meadow to Cloudy Pass at 6,438 ft. This is the line the recorded distance matches.
hazards: Spider Gap: permanent snow slope that can hold open crevasses and firm icy snow early season; axe and crampons
Whiteout or morning refreeze makes crampons necessary
Descending the steep first 100 ft north of the gap
Loose scree and shifting talus off the ridgeline; early-season snow on slopes
Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off

waysIn.name: Buck Creek Trail from Trinity, over Buck Creek Pass
waysIn.season: Jul–Sep
waysIn.notes: A longer alternative reaching Cloudy Pass from the Trinity Trailhead by way of Buck Creek Pass. One of the three ways in; it is a multi-day trip rather than a variation on the standard day.
hazards: Long multi-day approach over Buck Creek Pass
Ice axe and traction advised near the Lyman Glacier basin even in August
Loose scree and shifting talus off the ridgeline; early-season snow on slopes
Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the Trinity side and making a longer multi-day trip of it, instead of the shorter Phelps Creek day over Spider Gap.

waysIn.name: Railroad Creek from Holden Village
waysIn.season: Jul–Sep
waysIn.notes: Reaches Lower Lyman Lake and Cloudy Pass from Holden Village, which is itself reached by the Lake Chelan boat and a vehicle shuttle. The longest of the three and the one with the most fixed logistics.
hazards: Long approach reliant on ferry and shuttle logistics from Holden
Valley walk up Railroad Creek, then meadows to Cloudy Pass
Loose scree and shifting talus off the ridgeline; early-season snow on slopes
Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you are already based at Holden Village, reached by the Lake Chelan boat and a shuttle; the longest way in with the most fixed logistics.

name: West Face
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601, off Icicle Creek Road outside Leavenworth; NW Forest Pass required). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge around the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) splits left. Continue on #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek again on a second log bridge, then climb increasingly steep, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain from the trailhead, roughly 1:45-2:00 for a fit party with a rack). From the lake there are two ways into the west basin below Colchuck Balanced Rock (CBR): the shorter northern line crosses the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follows a climbers' path across a timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the west face (about an hour, plus roughly 20-25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the actual base); the longer southern/Aasgard option follows the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, cuts north through a band of slide alder (look for cairns), then climbs the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top before contouring east on an easy path into the basin (1.5-2 hours total, more elevation gain but avoids the outlet ford). Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water; the basin and route itself are dry. Hazards: the Mountaineer Creek log-bridge crossings can be slick or partially submerged in high early-season flow, the slide-alder section is a genuine bushwhack, the gully and basin talus are loose, and snow can linger in the gully well into early summer, making an ice axe/traction useful before mid-July.
descent: Descend the same way you climbed the upper pitches: from the top, scramble to a slung horn on the east side of the summit block and make one roughly 30-meter (about 100 ft) rappel — a single rope is sufficient, though some parties extend it with a doubled 60m for a lower touchdown. The anchor is a natural horn wrapped in webbing rather than bolts, so back it up or add your own sling if it looks tired; it sees heavy traffic and gets re-slung periodically. From the rappel's end, downclimb/scramble sandy scree and talus, working rightward (clockwise around the peak, roughly south then west) back into the basin and to your pack stash at the base of the west face — about 45 minutes to an hour car-to-base-equivalent. Some parties skip the rappel entirely and downclimb the same easy scree/snow line if conditions allow, since the terrain below the horn is low-angle. No further rappels are needed; this is the standard, single-rappel descent used for the West Face, The Scoop, and other CBR lines that top out on the summit block.
hazards: exposure on sustained upper pitches
very loose rock on the roped approach scramble
rockfall
afternoon thunderstorms typical of the east-Cascades summer

waysIn.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
waysIn.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake outlet, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges can be slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
The outlet crossing below the dam is a real crossing, not a step-across
Cirque talus is loose and the boulder-hop to the wall is ankle-breaking ground
Snow can linger in the approach terrain into early summer
No water above Colchuck Lake

waysIn.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
waysIn.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
waysIn.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.
hazards: Slide alder band is a real bushwhack; cairns are the only guide
1,000 ft of loose gully
Lingering snow in the gully into early summer
More elevation gain than the outlet approach
No water above Colchuck Lake
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the lake outlet crossing looks unreasonable; it avoids the ford but means a brushy bushwhack and a gully that can hold snow into early summer, so it takes longer.

name: Colchuck Glacier
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FS Road 7601, Eightmile Road, ~3,400 ft — reached via Icicle Road/FS 76 from Leavenworth, roughly 8.4 miles, then FS 7601 another 3.8 miles), follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles/1,100 ft of gain to the signed fork; take the right/south branch (Colchuck Lake Trail) and climb steep switchbacks through boulders for another 1.6 miles/1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, about 4 miles and 2,200 ft from the trailhead — a popular, often-permitted overnight zone in the Enchantments quota area, so many parties camp here rather than pushing to the summit car-to-car). Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water. From the lake, follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail and climb talus (or snow early season) directly up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft — this is the standard, moderate line up the peak (3rd class/mod. snow) and doubles as the descent for the other two routes here. The glacier itself is not significantly crevassed but is frequently icy by mid-to-late season, so crampons and an axe (and a rope if any crevasses/moats have opened) are standard; stay right of the main rockfall line coming off the surrounding faces, especially in the morning-warming window. Ascend the glacier to Colchuck–Dragontail Col (Colchuck Col/Banshee Pass, ~8,200 ft), then scramble northwest on blocky terrain to the summit (8,705 ft).
descent: This is a walk-off — no rappels. Reverse the ascent line: descend the glacier (staying climber's left, away from the thin crevasse zone that has opened as the glacier has retreated) and back down the lateral moraine to Colchuck Lake, then follow the Colchuck Lake Trail and Stuart Lake Trail back to the trailhead. In early season with good snow cover, much of the glacier and the upper trail basin can be glissaded, which many parties use to save time — but glissading here carries the usual runout/collision risk of any steep snow slope, so glissade only with a self-arrest-ready ice axe and clear runout. By afternoon on warm days the glacier softens considerably (postholing, wet-slide potential on any residual snow slopes), so climbers doing this as a long day often aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon.
hazards: crevasses late season
wet-snow avalanches on hot afternoons
rockfall near the Colchuck-Dragontail col
postholing in soft afternoon snow

The lateral moraine/talus approach to the glacier has ordinary loose-scree and rockfall exposure typical of Cascades approaches; hidden crevasses persist under snow cover through early July on the Colchuck Glacier below
A persistent bergschrund forms near the top of the Colchuck Glacier at the col exit; crossing difficulty varies with seasonal snow bridging and the glacier surface becomes icy/hard by mid-late season

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
waysIn.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.
hazards: Loose scree and talus if you do not gain the moraine crest early
Rockfall off the surrounding faces onto the glacier, worst during the morning warm-up
Moats and thin bridging at the glacier margins
~100 ft of 40-degree snow below the col
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
Glissading the descent is normal here and is also how people get hurt — axe in hand, clear runout

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
waysIn.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
waysIn.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.
hazards: Bare sun-cupped ice: crampons and axe required, self-arrest unreliable
Open crevasses and moats at the glacier margins
Increased rockfall from the surrounding faces with no snow cover
No glissade descent — the day is longer at both ends
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late summer, when the glacier has melted to hard ice; needs crampons, often two tools, and a down-climb because the snow glissade is gone, so most parties prefer the early window.

name: Northeast Couloir
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FS Road 7601 (Eightmile Road), elevation ~3,400 ft — in early season when Eightmile Road is gated/snowed in, tack on roughly 4 additional miles of road walking/skiing from the Bridge Creek Campground area on Icicle Road. From the trailhead, follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles and 1,100 ft of gain to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail forks left; the Stuart Lake Trail continues straight to Stuart Lake/Colchuck Pass and is not your route. Climb the steep, rooty switchbacks of the Colchuck Lake Trail through boulder fields for another 1.6 miles and 1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4 miles and 2,200 ft from the car) — this is the only reliable water source below the basin, and it's your last easy resupply. Follow the trail and boot path along the lake's west shore to the inlet at the south end (~5 miles in). Leave the maintained trail here and ascend talus, heather benches, or lingering snow (highly season-dependent) up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft. Rather than heading up-glacier toward Colchuck/Banshee Col (that's the Colchuck Glacier route), traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the main fall line under the north face and Northeast Buttress to limit rockfall and icefall exposure. The Northeast Couloir's entrance is the obvious narrow slot higher up the glacier than the North Buttress Couloir, directly below the Northeast Buttress; gaining it typically requires crossing a moat at the glacier's edge, which varies from a simple step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer. Expect avalanche-prone slopes above the lake in spring/early-summer conditions, and increasing rockfall down the couloir itself as the day warms.
descent: Standard descent is the walk-off: from the summit, traverse/downclimb to the Colchuck–Dragontail col (Colchuck Col, also called Banshee Pass) and descend the Colchuck Glacier's east/true-right lobe back to the basin above Colchuck Lake, then reverse the approach trail — the same line used to descend the Colchuck Glacier route. This is the recommended way down; reversing through the Northeast Couloir itself is discouraged because of loose rock in the entry gully and awkward mixed downclimbing. That said, some parties (particularly ski descents or parties that got benighted) do reverse the couloir instead of the full glacier walk-off: accounts describe downclimbing back to the top of the upper rock band, then either downclimbing it (not recommended) or making a single ~50m rappel off a natural anchor (you'll likely need to build one from boulders/slings — nothing fixed is documented) down to a ledge system on the southeast face; from there, a gully just east of the couloir's top can be down-climbed or rappelled with two or three single-strand 30m raps (again on natural/rigged anchors) to reach easier snow slopes, from which you continue down into the basin. Treat this as an emergency/alternate option, not the primary plan. No rappels are needed on the standard Colchuck Glacier walk-off descent; the main hazards there are a possible moat step-across near the col and glissade-glazed or icy snow by midsummer.
hazards: avalanche in the confined couloir
spindrift during and after storms
rockfall as the aspect warms
cornice barring the exit
a steep entry/exit crux reported up to 60 degrees

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow and ice climb; by high summer the entry moat opens and the couloir sheds rock
waysIn.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction and fork left for Colchuck Lake — straight on goes to Stuart Lake and a different valley. Switchback up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles and 2,200 ft in, and fill water: it is the last easy source. Take the trail and boot path along the lake's west shore to the inlet at the south end. Leave the trail there and climb talus, heather benches or snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Now the important part. Do not continue up-glacier toward the col — that is the Colchuck Glacier route. Traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the fall line under the face. If Eightmile Road is gated in early season, add roughly four miles of road each way.
hazards: Rockfall down the couloir once the sun reaches the face
An entry moat that can require an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer
Avalanche-prone slopes above Colchuck Lake in spring and early summer
Steep snow and ice to 60-plus degrees at the exit
Reversing the couloir is discouraged — plan on the Colchuck Glacier walk-off, which is long

name: Cosley-Houston Couloir
approach: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (~3,700 ft, end of Glacier Creek Road/FR 39), follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail (#677) through forest for roughly 2 miles, crossing a plank bridge over Grouse Creek and one avalanche-path/rockfall gully below Hogsback that can hold hazardous debris and running water in warm conditions. The trail breaks out of trees near a viewpoint of Coleman Glacier icefall around 4,900-5,000 ft; this is the last reliable running water before the moraine. From there, gain the lateral moraine and the well-worn Coleman-Deming boot track (the standard Mount Baker route), staying on or near the crest of the moraine before dropping onto glacier ice. Rope up for glacier travel here — crevasse hazard is real and grows through the season. Contour/ascend the Coleman Glacier heading climber's right (northeast) toward the prominent bench/rognon beneath the north faces of Colfax Peak, staying low and left around a well-known large crevasse that guards the direct line; parties commonly reach this bench in 3 to 4.5 hours from the car with good booting conditions, slower after new snow or when the skin track has been chewed up by skiers. Total gain to the route base near 8,000 ft is on the order of 4,500-4,700 ft over roughly 4-5 miles one-way; the upper glacier and bergschrund crossing should be done early before the north-facing slopes see any sun-warming, and this route/aspect avalanches after new snow, so avoid climbing after significant snowfall or in elevated avalanche danger.
descent: Cosley-Houston is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. From the summit area, follow the boot track (or break a new one) toward Colfax's secondary/eastern summit, then contour around its south side just below the top — no technical downclimbing is required on a normal-conditions descent. This drops you to the Colfax-Baker col (the Baker-Colfax saddle). From the saddle, pick up the standard Coleman-Deming route down the Coleman Glacier, roping up again and watching for the same crevasses navigated on the way up (some parties note trending to the glacier's right side to find solid bridges late-season). Continue down to the moraine, then the Heliotrope Ridge Trail back to the trailhead. Give yourself a real daylight margin for this: parties specifically warn against descending the glacier after dark, and parties that summit late have ended up down-climbing the icy trail by headlamp. There is no rappelling on the standard descent.
hazards: Steep ice couloir with rockfall once it warms
Bergschrund at the base
Loose rock on the exit and upper mountain
Large, well-known crevasse on the Coleman Glacier approach -- stay lower/climber's-left
Poor, "kitty-litter" rock quality at some belay/rappel anchors

waysIn.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 and the Coleman Glacier to the bench beneath the north faces
waysIn.season: Roughly Oct-May. This is a cold-season route: it wants the north faces frozen, and it avalanches after new snow
waysIn.notes: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR-39) near 3,700 ft, follow Trail #677 about two miles through forest, over a plank bridge on Grouse Creek and across one avalanche path below Hogsback that can hold debris and running water in warm conditions. The trail breaks out of trees near the Coleman icefall viewpoint around 4,900-5,000 ft — the last reliable running water before the moraine. Gain the lateral moraine and the well-worn Coleman-Deming boot track, staying on or near the moraine crest before dropping onto ice. Rope up here. Contour and ascend the Coleman climber's right — northeast — toward the bench beneath Colfax's north faces, staying low and left around the large crevasse that guards the direct line. Parties in good booting conditions commonly reach the bench in three to four and a half hours from the car. Four routes share this bench.
hazards: An overhanging bergschrund that is the crux obstacle of the approach in lean years
Avalanche on this aspect after any new snow — do not climb it on a loaded slope
Crevasses on the Coleman, including one large one that guards the direct line to the bench
Sun-warming of the north faces later in the day, so the schrund must be crossed early
A glacier descent that multiple parties specifically warn against doing after dark

name: West Ridge / Colonial Glacier
approach: Start at the signed Pyramid Lake Trailhead on SR 20 (small pullout on the north side of the highway, ~21 miles east of Marblemount and just past the Diablo turnoff, elev. ~1,150 ft; no parking pass needed, NPS backcountry permit if camping). Follow the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail — a well-used boot path through second-growth and old-growth forest — which climbs a steady, unrelenting ~1,500-1,600 ft over about 2.1-2.3 miles to Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft). This maintained-trail portion ends at the lake; everything above is climbers'-trail/off-trail travel. Pick up the boot path around the right (east/north) side of the lake and continue climbing, now through brush, heather, and talus, gaining roughly 2,000 more feet up onto the crest of Pyramid Ridge. A knoll around 5,400-5,500 ft on this ridge is the customary high camp/bivy — seasonal ponds and puddles here and near ~4,500 ft (reported dry by late summer in low-snow years) are the last reliable water before the glacier. From the ridge crest, follow the climbers' path along the ridge over several knolls toward the base of Pyramid Peak, then drop and traverse a mix of scree and boulder-hop terrain beneath Pyramid's crumbly north face to reach the flat 6,100 ft basin at the toe of the Colonial Glacier — this traverse is loose underfoot and exposed to rockfall from above, and is the route's main approach-specific hazard. From the glacier-toe basin, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the Colonial Glacier, trending southeast/east across the upper glacier (crevasses are usually well-bridged under seasonal snow but are present and have been reported as a hazard, along with cornices along the traverse toward the Colonial-Snowfield col that are invisible from camp below) to reach the Colonial-Snowfield col or the base of the historic Northeast Gully. From the col, leave the ice for a loose gully leading up onto the West Ridge, which is then followed via Class 3-4 rock scrambling to the summit horn. Total car-to-summit distance runs roughly 10-14 miles round trip (parties differ depending on camp placement) with the ~6,600 ft of gain split roughly evenly between the maintained trail, the ridge/scree traverse, and the glacier-to-summit push.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the east ridge back to the head of the Northeast Gully, then downclimb/plunge-step the snow gully back down to the Colonial-Snowfield col, drop back onto the Colonial Glacier, and retrace the rope-up glacier traverse and the loose scree/boulder traverse beneath Pyramid Peak back to the Pyramid Ridge camp, then follow the climbers' path and maintained Pyramid Lake Trail back to the car. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel-dependent descent — but on the class 3-4 rock near the summit ridge, trip reports document an existing rap station (a sling/webbing anchor around a rock horn, not bolted) that some parties use for a short single-rope rappel (roughly 20-30m, any single rope 30m+ works) over the steepest step; other parties simply downclimb this same section instead, since it's optional class 3-4 terrain for a confident scrambler. There is no other fixed or bolted rappel infrastructure reported on this route. Descent hazards mirror the approach in reverse: softening glacier snow and weaker crevasse bridges later in the day, loose rock in the gully and on the summit ridge scramble, potential rockfall on the Pyramid traverse, and the reported cornice hazard along the glacier traverse near the col — parties should time the glacier/col crossing for firm early-morning or evening snow rather than midday.
hazards: crevasse fall on the Colonial Glacier
steep snow
exposed summit rock
moat gaps at the glacier's rock margins, worse late season

waysIn.name: Pyramid Lake, the 5,800 ft notch, and the traverse to the glacier toe
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead the maintained trail ends at the lake around 2,600 ft; above that a climbers' path follows the ridgeline to the notch under Pyramid Peak at about 5,800 ft. Near the top of the now-open ridge, take the path that veers left down a cedar bench and forested ledge, using cedar pulls and low-grade rock scrambling to drop into the Colonial Creek basin. Two ways across: a high line holding roughly 5,800 ft, or a lower one that gives up some height but keeps a good boot path and regains it just before the Colonial Creek waterfall. Where the trail opens onto rock slabs below Pyramid Peak, head climber's left across the talus fields toward the ice. A large tarn sits at the northwest toe of the glacier and makes a good water source and camp.
hazards: The talus traverse under Pyramid Peak's crumbly north face is loose and exposed to rockfall from above
Crevasses on the Colonial Glacier, usually bridged under seasonal snow but present
Cornices on the traverse toward the col that are invisible from camp below
Loose rock and real exposure on the upper ridge

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Verlot Public Service Center, continue east on the (now fully paved) Mountain Loop Highway roughly 19.5 miles to the large Barlow Pass trailhead/parking area (permit required). From the parking lot, follow the old Monte Cristo mining road — gated to public vehicles — east for about 4 miles (roughly 500 ft of gentle gain); this stretch is popular to mountain-bike to save time and is a fairly flat, wide roadbed with one notable washout-prone reroute near the start and a South Fork Sauk River crossing (log/footbridge) about a mile in. The road ends at the Monte Cristo ghost-town townsite (old mining buildings, informal camping). Pick up the signed Poodle Dog Pass/Twin Lakes trail behind the townsite and climb switchbacks about 1.5 miles and 1,600 ft to Poodle Dog Pass, passing Silver Lake. From the pass, continue on the Twin Lakes Trail — mostly well-graded but with occasional deadfall — to Twin Lakes (a popular basin for overnight scramblers), crossing granite slabs on the final approach; Sunday Creek, about 1.25 miles before the lakes, is the last reliable water source before the climb. From Twin Lakes (~5,000 ft), leave the trail and go cross-country up the east side/east crest of East Twin Peak, dropping into boulder fields around 5,300-5,800 ft, then trending up heather benches below cliff bands. Above roughly 6,300 ft the route works past a buttress via one of two class 3-4 options (a crack/chimney move on the left, or an easier move right into a ~50-ft gully) — this short section has minimal exposure but the gully above is steep with loose rock, so parties should stay close together and wear helmets. Above the gully, class 2-3 slabs and scree lead across the southwest face to the base of the summit block, finishing with a short class 3 corkscrew move around the final cliff band to the top. Route-finding through the boulder fields and buttress is the main crux of the approach; snow lingering into early summer on the upper ledges makes the route significantly more hazardous and it's best attempted after it has melted out.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly — this is a downclimb/walk-off with no rappelling anywhere on the route (rappels: 0). From the summit block, reverse the class 3 corkscrew moves and downclimb the southwest-facing slabs and scree back to the buttress; reverse the class 3-4 crack/chimney (or the gully move used on the way up), taking care with loose rock in the gully — do not descend directly below other party members. Continue down through the heather benches and boulder fields back to Twin Lakes, then follow the Twin Lakes Trail over Poodle Dog Pass and down to Monte Cristo, and retrace the old mining road (or coast it on a bike) back to Barlow Pass. Parties note the descent typically goes noticeably faster than the ascent once the route-finding through the boulder fields/buttress is known (some parties report under 3 hours down vs. 4+ up). Main descent hazards are the same loose gully/buttress terrain as on the ascent and, in shoulder season, lingering snow on the ledge traverse below the summit.
hazards: long Monte Cristo approach
routefinding
afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: Twin Lakes saddle and the west spur
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Twin Lakes saddle around 5,000 ft, leave the trail and go cross-country up the east side and east crest of East Twin Peak. Most parties never reach the lakes: a distinct path forges off to the left somewhere between about 5,200 and 5,400 ft, roughly a hundred feet below the junction where the way trail drops into the lake basin, and taking it saves several hundred feet of regain. Traverse talus and heather toward a dip in the ridge, follow the bootpath up through boulders, rock, scree and heather, then stay close to the ridge crest across a meadow and a gravelly slope, keeping high. On the connecting ridge stay LOW rather than crossing its crest — climbing over the top has been tried and reported as a poor idea.
hazards: Loose rock in the gully above the buttress — keep the party close together and wear helmets
Snow lingering on the upper ledges into early summer makes the route significantly more hazardous
Route-finding through the boulder fields in cloud
A tiny ledge with a big runout just below the final summit scramble

name: Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer
approach: From Highway 530 in Darrington, go south on Madison Avenue to the T, turn right on Darrington Street and follow it as it becomes Squire Creek Road (FS 2040) to the washout that blocks it. Walk or bike the old roadbed past the landslide crossing to the Squire Creek Trail #654 sign, then continue 8–10 minutes to two cut logs on either side of the track, with old logging cable low and just right of it. A few steps past the logs, turn right on a well-beaten boot track down to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest — hard in early season or after storms. Across the creek, follow a climbers' track right (downstream); it soon turns uphill, crosses a tributary (also hard early in the season), climbs through old-growth forest and drops left into two gullies, which it follows up. The top of the second gully is steep and dirty and opens onto a grassy saddle with good bivy sites, near the start of Concerto. Allow about 3 hours from the car. This turn-off comes before the one for Waterfall Basin, which is farther along at a wide streambed of white boulders.
descent: Rappel the line of ascent on fixed chain/bolt anchors; parties typically rappel to the Pitch 13 chain anchor near the summit before continuing down.
hazards: Sustained low-angle friction slab is unforgiving if wet
Steep, brushy, poorly maintained approach with stream crossings and old rockslide/avalanche debris

waysIn.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
waysIn.season: Summer; the boot track is steep and dirty and the saddle bivy is snow-free only in high summer
waysIn.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington go south on Madison Ave to a T, right onto Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and drive to the washout that gates it.

Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing and on toward the old trailhead. The South Face turn-off is a made object, not a natural feature: look for two cut logs, one on either side of the road, with old logging cable visible. At those logs turn right onto a well-beaten boot track.

The boot track drops to the creek for a ford, then climbs steeply through old-growth forest. The upper part is steep and dirty before it breaks out into open grassland. Around three hours from the trailhead to the main bivy.

This is a different turn-off from Waterfall Basin, which is further along at the wide white-boulder streambed. Two cut logs with cable = South Face; 50-foot streambed of white boulders = Waterfall Basin.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek on the boot track
Steep, dirty ground in the upper forest
Long approach with no maintained trail above the cut logs

name: North Face
approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20, about 0.5 mile past milepost 162 and about 1 mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-graded, well-maintained Blue Lake Trail through forest and past small tarns/streams for roughly 1.5-2 miles as it climbs into the open basin below the Liberty Bell group. Watch on your left (south/east side of the trail) for a signed, well-trodden climbers' path (Liberty Bell Trail #727) branching off shortly after the trail crosses a small stream near a meadow — this is easy to miss if you're not looking for it, and is the standard access to the Liberty Bell / Concord Tower massif rather than continuing on to Blue Lake itself. The climbers' path climbs steeply through slabs, talus, and heather meadow into upper 'Liberty Bowl,' gaining roughly 1,900-2,000 ft from the trailhead (figure 1.5-2.5 hours from the trailhead depending on fitness and snow conditions) to reach the gully/notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (the Liberty Bell-Concord col, roughly 7,400 ft). This entry gully is frequently snow-filled and can stay icy into late June — many early-season parties carry an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) for it. Because the gully's rock is held together by snow much of the season, rockfall risk rises noticeably once the snow melts out, so helmet up before entering it and be mindful of parties above/below. The North Face route begins essentially at the top of this notch.
descent: Descend by rappelling back down the North Face line itself — do not try to walk off. From the summit, move to the double-bolt rap chains (a short, slightly awkward step/slither over the summit block gets you to the anchor) and make three single-rope rappels with a 60m rope: rappel 1 goes from the summit chains down the upper face; rappel 2 starts from a bolted anchor just below Pitch 3's 5.0 slab section and drops to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge atop Pitch 1; rappel 3 goes from that ledge back to the base of the climb at the notch. The first two stations are fixed bolts/chains; the last, on the pitch-1 ledge, is a tree or bush, so carry webbing and a rap ring. From the base, reverse the approach: descend the gully/climbers' path back through Liberty Bowl to the Blue Lake Trail and out to the trailhead. Note this is distinct from the South Face descent option some parties use when linking Concord with Lexington Tower — that alternate line is only 2 rappels but the first is a full 30m pull requiring the rope's middle mark to be set correctly at the anchor; the direct North Face descent described here is the standard 3-rappel version.
hazards: Concord Tower is reached off the loose Beckey/Liberty-Concord Gully, which carries rockfall potential, especially during spring/early-summer melt-out through late June.
About 10-15 ft of essentially unprotected (though juggy/hueco-featured) climbing on pitch 2, plus hollow- and flaky-sounding rock in sections of that pitch.
The summit tower is small and exposed; manage loose blocks on belay ledges.
Often climbed in combination with Liberty Bell, adding traffic and rope-induced rockfall.

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass; about 1.75 miles of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.
hazards: loose, heavily trafficked gully below the notch — helmets, and don't queue underneath another party
hollow-sounding flakes on the upper pitches send debris to the notch
no water above the stream at the Trail #727 junction

waysIn.name: Early-season snow to the notch
waysIn.season: Highway opening through late Jun
waysIn.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.
hazards: firm snow in the gully with a long runout below
moat between snow and rock at the base
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access until the highway reopens
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early in the season, once the highway reopens and before the gully melts out; it needs an axe and perhaps crampons, but the rock stays frozen in place and rockfall is lower.

name: South Route
approach: Copper Peak has no drivable trailhead — access is via the Lake Chelan ferry from Fields Point/Chelan to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up to Holden Village (~3,300 ft) in the Railroad Creek valley, Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the village, follow the old mine road/Railroad Creek Trail east roughly 0.5 mile and cross Railroad Creek (footbridge or ford, depending on season) to reach a large tailings pile at about 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off. This climbers'/boot trail climbs steeply for about 0.7 mile up a hillside (partly burned) before entering the Copper Creek drainage, then parallels the creek south for roughly 3 miles, gaining to about 5,600 ft where it crosses a flat, open bench — this is the standard base camp (Copper Basin) used by nearly all parties. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft, but a continuing boot path pushes on toward the Copper–Entiat Divide near 7,200 ft. From camp, leave the trail, ford Copper Creek to its west side, and traverse/ascend talus and slabs alongside the outlet stream draining the Southeast Glacier remnant on the peak's east face. Reliable water is available along Railroad and Copper Creeks and near camp, but carry what you need above the basin. Hazards include two creek crossings that run higher and faster during early-season snowmelt, a steep and unmaintained burned-hillside section just above the valley floor, loose Class 3 talus/scree approaching the glacier, and real crevasse hazard on the (much-diminished but still present) Southeast Glacier — rope up for glacier travel, especially early in the season. Above the glacier a loose Class 3 gully gains a notch on the ridge's north side; a steep snowfield/snow gully beyond can require crampons and, if icy, a belay. The high camp near 6,500 ft has running water beside it and flat room for about one two-person tent (late August).
descent: Nearly all parties reverse the ascent line (Southeast Glacier / upper Northeast Ridge route) rather than finding a separate walk-off: downclimb the Class 3 ridge (one short, more exposed Class 3+/4 move is commonly reported near the summit ridge, and some parties carry a short hand line for one airy notch — this is a fixed handline, not a rappel) back to the north-side notch, downclimb (or belay, if icy) the steep snowfield/gully back onto the Southeast Glacier remnant, cross the glacier roped and mindful of crevasses, descend the loose Class 3 gully back into the upper basin, then retrace the boot path and Copper Creek Trail to Holden Village. Multiple trip reports for this route explicitly describe downclimbing the ascent line — one notes glissading available snow where possible — and none report rappelling; this is a downclimb/walk-off route, not a rappel descent.
hazards: loose class 3-4 rock in the ridge-notch gully
rockfall
remote, multi-day self-rescue terrain with no cell service
standing dead timber/deadfall in an old burn along the Copper Creek approach trail

waysIn.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
waysIn.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large tailings pile around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its west side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
