hazards: No drivable trailhead; ferry and shuttle logistics, closed by a recent flood and landslide
Creek crossings run high in early season; one depends on a footbridge that may be out
Standing dead timber and loose footing on the steep burned hillside above the tailings
Several notches in the spur ridge, most Class 5 from below; picking the wrong one is the crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier, worst late summer
Loose Class 3-4 gully to the notch and a short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge
Very remote, no cell service, multi-day self-rescue

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
waysIn.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead, walk up through Spider Meadow and the Spider Glacier to Spider Gap, drop past the Lyman Glacier to Lyman Lake, then follow the Railroad Creek trail down the valley to Copper Creek. It avoids the boat and shuttle but is far longer, with a steep snow climb to the gap.
hazards: Far longer approach with a steep snow climb to Spider Gap
Descent past Lyman Glacier, then a long valley walk to Copper Creek
Burned hillside with standing dead timber and loose footing on the Copper Creek trail
Several notches in the spur ridge, most Class 5 from below; picking the wrong one is the crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the glacier remnant, worst late summer
Loose Class 3-4 gully and a short exposed Class 4 step; very remote, no cell service
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the Lake Chelan ferry and Holden shuttle are not running; far longer, with a steep snow climb to Spider Gap, so it suits strong parties who can commit to a multi-day trip.

name: Southwest Ridge / Standard Route
approach: From the paved pullout at Rainy Pass (4,855 ft) on SR-20 — signed 'Rainy Pass Trailhead,' 52 miles east of Marblemount, right where the PCT crosses the highway — start on the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (well-graded, heavily used). At roughly 1.25 miles, stay right at the Lake Ann junction (the lake itself, just below the junction, is the last reliable on-trail water source) and continue climbing switchbacks through heather meadows to Heather Pass (~6,080 ft, about 2 miles in), Leave the maintained trail here and head west across talus, keeping south of Lewis Lake (~5,700 ft), to the crest of the Lewis Glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Follow the moraine onto the glacier remnant and climb southeast, bearing left near the top, to a notch in the ridge at about 7,500 ft. Work west along the ridge to a second notch, downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the cirque under the west face, then take an easy gully up to a large notch on the Southwest Ridge and follow the crest (exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves) to the 8,107 ft summit. Loose talus and scree cover much of the off-trail travel, and the downclimb sheds rock onto anyone below, so a helmet is worth carrying. Snow lingers on the glacier and on the traverse out of Heather Pass well into July, so bring an axe and crampons for early-season attempts.
descent: The standard descent reverses the same Southwest Ridge line used on ascent, down into the west-face cirque. From the summit, downclimb blocky, exposed class 3 (with a few class 4 moves) south/southwest along the ridge crest to a large notch roughly a third of the way down (approximately 7,600-7,700 ft), reached through an easy connecting gully. That gully has one distinctly steeper step, which is the crux of the way down: most parties downclimb it as class 4 on solid holds, but it is commonly protected with a single-strand rappel (one 30 m rope is sufficient) off natural gear — horns, chockstones, or a sling around a block; no fixed or bolted anchor has been reported here, so carry a few slings/cord. Treat this as optional but be ready for it, especially if the rock is wet or the party is not comfortable down-climbing exposed class 4. Below the step, follow the gully and talus down into the west-face cirque near the Lewis Glacier's east moraine (~6,400 ft), then pick up talus and intermittent boot path south past Lewis Lake to rejoin the trail near Heather Pass. From Heather Pass it's about 2 miles of maintained trail back down to the Rainy Pass Trailhead. This line involves glacier/snowfield travel past the Lewis Glacier remnant — rope up or use an axe/crampons if it's icy — and lingering snow on these slopes can be avalanche-prone in early summer. Total descent is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,250 ft of net loss back to the car.
hazards: loose blocks and variable rock quality on the ridge
narrow, sand-covered ledges with precariously perched snow blocks (reported in multiple trip reports)
steep snow/rock step (up to ~70 degrees) below the ~7,500 ft ridge notch
crevasses on the Lewis Glacier, especially early season
early-season approach snow
afternoon thunderstorms over the crest in summer
mountain goats on the ridge and near camp (habituated, can be assertive around salt/water)

waysIn.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then Lewis Lake and the Lewis Glacier moraine
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct
waysIn.notes: From the Rainy Pass trailhead (4,855 ft) on SR-20, 52 miles east of Marblemount where the PCT crosses the highway, take the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail. This is the Rainy Pass Lake Ann, not the one below Mount Shuksan. At roughly 1.25 miles stay right at the Lake Ann junction; the lake just below it is the last reliable on-trail water. Switchbacks through heather meadows lead to Heather Pass at about 6,080 ft, roughly 2 miles in, where the maintained trail ends and the off-trail travel to Lewis Lake and the glacier begins.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the off-trail travel beyond Heather Pass
Snow, bare ice and moats on the Lewis Glacier remnant; carry an axe and crampons early season
Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass well into July
Loose ground on the 400 ft downclimb into the west-face cirque; move one at a time
One distinctly steeper class 4 step on the descent, with no fixed anchor reported
Lake Ann is the last reliable on-trail water

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on the south side of SR 20 (Easy Pass Trail, North Cascades National Park, backcountry permit required for camping). The trail climbs steadily through forest, crossing Easy Pass Creek three times, and breaks out into subalpine meadows and heather benches before the final push to Easy Pass at about 6,550 ft — roughly 3.5-3.6 miles and 2,700-2,800 ft of gain, typically 2-3 hours. Steep snow can linger on this stretch well into July, and an ice axe is recommended; the tread can be hard to follow across snowfields, and the meadows are fragile, so stay on trail/rock where possible. From the pass, leave the high traverse and descend the Fisher Creek side: the trail switchbacks roughly 30 times, losing nearly 1,400 ft, into the Fisher Creek valley. Follow the Fisher Creek Trail west/downstream along the north side of the creek for about 3 miles (the creek itself is a reliable water source) to Cosho Camp (~3,900-4,200 ft, creekside, a designated NPS camping zone and the logical base camp for this peak). From Cosho Camp continue west on the trail roughly another mile until due south of the Cosho/Kimtah saddle, then leave the trail and begin climbing one of the gullies leading north, starting around 3,800 ft. This off-trail leg is the crux of the approach: steep talus, grass, and some solid rock for about 4,000 ft of gain to a saddle at roughly 7,830 ft, with sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush in the first thousand feet and loose, tedious scree higher up. Alternatively, some parties camp higher, in a basin south of Mesahchie Peak (~6,600 ft) reached by traversing south of the Easy Pass ridge at 6,600-6,700 ft across numerous small gullies and buttresses (~1 mile, ~5 hours from the trailhead), then climb about 800 ft to a 7,400 ft bench and traverse west to the Cosho/Kimtah col — a shorter final push at the cost of a longer, more exposed high traverse to reach camp. Expect this to be a full, long trekking day regardless of which camp is used; this is a remote, seldom-visited corner of the park and route-finding care is needed in poor visibility.
descent: This is a scramble, not a technical rock route, and no rappels are used — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-4 upper section back to the saddle (accounts vary on the exact character here: some parties describe a short, fun class 2-3 scramble from a notch just below the true summit; others describe roughly 250 vertical feet of class 3-4 terrain near the top, including an airy, exposed 4th-class ledge system that requires careful downclimbing, 250-300 ft, back toward the col). From the ~7,830 ft saddle, downclimb the steep talus/grass/brush gully back to about 3,800 ft where you rejoin the Fisher Creek Trail, then retrace the approach: east on the Fisher Creek Trail past Cosho Camp, back up the ~1,400 ft of switchbacks to Easy Pass, and down the Easy Pass Trail to the trailhead. Loose rock and scree on the gully descent are the main hazard — care is needed not to kick rock onto party members below — and lingering snow in the upper gullies/saddle area into midsummer may warrant an ice axe and caution on the downclimb. No rappel gear is required for this route under normal summer conditions.
hazards: loose rock
remote position with long approach
steep snow on Easy Pass's north side and the Kimtah-Cosho saddle approach (ice axe recommended)
crevasses/moats on the Kimtah Glacier if approaching via the high Ragged Ridge traverse

waysIn.name: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft.
hazards: Four thousand feet of loose, brushy off-trail gain with no water above the creek
Firm snow on the north side of the saddle — carry an ice axe
Remote and rarely visited; navigating back to the correct gully in poor visibility is the real danger
The wrong gully on the way down leads into brush

waysIn.name: From Kimtah, down the south gully and the connecting traverse
waysIn.notes: This way is used by parties combining Cosho with Kimtah: they descend Kimtah's south gully and follow cairns down the connecting traverse to the same saddle.
waysIn.whyThisWay: When linking Cosho with Kimtah in one trip: after Kimtah, a cairned third-class traverse reaches the saddle, so you skip the steep brushy gully up from the Fisher Creek trail.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead (elev. ~3,960 ft, at the end of FR-4300-500 off East Buttermilk Creek Road/FR-43, reached via Twisp River Road west of Twisp), follow the West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs steadily up the West Fork of Buttermilk Creek through ponderosa pine and larch forest. Expect several unbridged crossings of the creek and its side drainages that can run high and fast with snowmelt through June — plan on wet feet or careful boulder-hopping in early season. Maintenance is light and blowdowns are common in the lower miles in recent years; a GPS track is worth carrying since flagging/tread can thin out where deadfall forces detours around downed timber. At roughly 7–7.5 miles and about 3,500 ft of cumulative gain, the trail tops out at Fish Creek Pass (~7,480 ft), a major junction where it meets the Fish Creek Trail #1248; Star Lake sits just below/north of the pass and is the last reliable water source before the summit push, and a common camp for parties splitting the trip over two days. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the obvious boot path/climbers' trail that switchbacks northwest up the open ridge toward Courtney Peak. This use trail gains roughly 900–1,000 ft on easy class 2 tundra and talus with a good game/climbers' path most of the way; a few hundred feet below the summit it steepens into larger class 2+ boulders that require careful hopping and some route-finding to the summit block. Snow can linger in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season (June) attempts. Round trip from trailhead to summit and back runs about 17 miles with roughly 4,700 ft of total gain — this matches a long car-to-car day or an overnight with camp at Star Lake, not the longer Star/Oval combined traverse some parties do as a multi-summit epic. Past the washout roughly three miles in, fallen trees still need to be climbed over in early October, and the creek is crossed on a log; flagging marks the easiest line through the washout.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: downclimb the class 2+ boulder field below the summit back onto the boot path, then follow the use trail down the southeast ridge to Fish Creek Pass. From the pass, rejoin the West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 for the full hike back down to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb the entire way — there is no rappelling on the standard route, and most parties do not carry a rope. The main descent hazards are the loose class 2+ talus just below the summit (careful foot placement, stay alert for rockfall onto parties below) and, near the pass and on the upper ridge, lingering snow or wet scree that can be slick into early summer — an ice axe/microspikes are useful insurance in June. Some parties link Courtney with Star Peak and/or Oval Peak and descend via a different drainage (e.g., toward Eagle Creek) as part of a car-shuttle loop, but that requires a second vehicle staged at a different trailhead and is a variation on, not the standard version of, this out-and-back route.
hazards: loose talus
long approach to the Sawtooth crest
unsecured/wobbly log crossing of West Fork Buttermilk Creek near the trailhead

waysIn.name: West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 to Fish Creek Pass
waysIn.season: Late June through early October; a popular early-October objective for larch colour along the crest. Snow lingers in the gullies off the crest into July.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the spur off East Buttermilk Creek Road, sign in at the wilderness register and follow Trail #411 up the West Fork valley through ponderosa and larch. The creek is crossed unbridged within the first half mile on unsecured, often wobbly downed logs, and several more crossings follow — all of them push hard with snowmelt through June. Maintenance is light and blowdown is common in the lower miles, so expect detours where the flagging and tread both thin out. The trail climbs steadily to Fish Creek Pass, where it tops out and meets the Fish Creek Trail; Star Lake sits just below the far side and is the last reliable water and the usual high camp.
hazards: Unbridged creek crossings on unsecured logs, worst during June snowmelt
Heavy blowdown in the lower miles where the tread and flagging both disappear
Lingering snow in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July
Loose class 2+ blocks in the last few hundred feet where the boot path breaks up
No water above Star Lake

name: Standard Route (Southeast Ridge via Jackita Ridge / Crater Lake Trail)
approach: From the Canyon Creek Trailhead (1,900 ft) on SR 20 (32.8 mi east of Marblemount / 55.1 mi west of Winthrop), take Jackita Ridge Trail #738, crossing Granite Creek on a bridge and fording Canyon Creek near the start. The trail climbs steeply through timber via numerous switchbacks (roughly 55) gaining about 3,400 ft over 4 miles to a junction near 5,000-5,260 ft, with views opening onto Crater and Jack Mountains above timberline. Turn left onto the Crater Lake Trail (brushy, user-maintained) for about a mile to Crater Lake (about 5,800 ft) below the peak's south side.
descent: From the summit, descend the scree/talus slopes back to the top of the crux gully and downclimb it carefully, following the same painted yellow X's/arrows and cairns used on the ascent (parties note this section is loose and exposure-sensitive both ways). Continue around the false summit's west side back onto the southeast ridge, drop into Crater Lake basin, and rejoin Jackita Ridge Trail for the descent to the Canyon Creek Trailhead, re-fording Canyon Creek.
hazards: Loose rock ("choss") through the crux gully and surrounding cliff bands is the primary objective hazard on this route.
A small grizzly bear population is present in the Pasayten Wilderness; standard bear-aware practices apply.

waysIn.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
waysIn.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. There is no bridge over Canyon Creek on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is unsigned, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the south shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.
hazards: An unbridged Canyon Creek ford, hazardous in spring and early summer, with no fixed crossing point
Yellow paint marks that lead into a steep, loose gully rather than along the better line
Loose rock through the scramble section, reported by most parties
No water above Crater Lake
Broken glass and nails around the old lookout remains on the east peak

waysIn.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
waysIn.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it exists to avoid the Canyon Creek ford. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.
hazards: A three-day committing loop with substantial cumulative gain
Same loose gully and misleading paint above
Long stretches with no bail-out
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the Canyon Creek ford looks too risky, as in spring or early summer; it trades the day trip for a roughly 48-mile, three-day loop over Devils Dome.

name: Cauthorn-Wilson Couloir
approach:
This route is on the east face, so the approach is the South Buttress approach with one extra step. From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, take the cairned climbers' track from its east end, drop through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

From there, cross the rib that runs south from the South Buttress into the basin east of the peak. Once you are in the right basin there is no ambiguity about the line — the objective is the large couloir splitting the East Face, and it is the dominant gully on that aspect. The error to avoid here is a basin error, not a gully error.

Usually climbed soon after SR-20 reopens, typically April into May.
descent: Many teams choose to rappel back down the couloir/ridgeline itself, building anchors on rock (some pre-existing/fixed) or building V-threads in the ice where present. Parties who continue to the true summit instead descend via the standard West Ridge descent used by the rock routes.
hazards: Avalanche danger on the approach and lower couloir, particularly later in the day or later in the season as solar input increases.
Variable ice quality year to year given the route's dependence on a narrow spring weather window.

waysIn.name: State Creek approach, then over the rib into the east basin
waysIn.season: Soon after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr-May
waysIn.notes:
This route is on the east face of Cutthroat Peak, and the approach is the South Buttress approach with an extra step. Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, find the cairned climbers' track leaving the east end of it, drop through timber and cross State Creek, then climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

From there, cross over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress and drop into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak. That crossing is what separates this approach from the rock-route approach, and it is the part with no boot path.

The route is in condition for a short window right after the highway opens each spring, usually April or May. SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated all winter — typically closing late November or early December and reopening mid-April to early May — so the season starts when the gate does.
hazards: east-facing slopes take sun for most of the day — serious avalanche and wet-slide concern, and a strong argument for a very early start
no established path across the rib into the east basin
State Creek crossing in spring melt
short seasonal window tied to the SR-20 opening

name: West Ridge
approach:
Park on the broad shoulder of SR-20 roughly half a mile west of the Blue Lake trailhead, where there is a view through the trees to the peak; parties often meet at the Blue Lake lot and drive the short distance west to it. Head up from there into the basin below the peak.

Coming up into the basin, stay somewhat left to arrive at the notch at the base of the west ridge. That notch, rather than the ridge crest above it, is the reference point — from it, traverse ledges for about a hundred feet to the foot of a shallow gully running up and left onto the ridge.
descent: Most parties reverse the ridge with short downclimbs and rappels from bolted anchors, the first just west of the summit, and rappel into the southwest gully at the foot of the ridge. Below the gully, drop skier's right onto a sandy rib with a faint climbers' track, then into another gully farther skier's right for the lower part; going straight down leads into loose ground. Pick up the climbers' path through the State Creek brush back to the highway.
hazards: The upper west ridge is exposed and has loose sections requiring care.
Early-season snow on the approach can complicate gaining the ridge.
Short technical pitches near the top mean a rope and small rack are worthwhile.

waysIn.name: Roadside pullout west of the Blue Lake Trailhead
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
There is a broad shoulder with room to park on SR-20 roughly half a mile west of the Blue Lake Trailhead, with a view through the trees to the peak. Parties commonly meet at the Blue Lake lot and then drive the short distance west to this pullout.

From there head up into the basin below the peak. Reported round-trip times are on the order of six hours up and four hours down for the whole climb, so this is a long day even though the walk-in is short.

On the way out, the descent line drops skier's right onto a sandy rib with a faint climbers' track, then into another gully further skier's right for the lower part — going straight down instead puts you into loose ground.
hazards: loose rock throughout the ridge and on the descent gullies
long day relative to the short approach
route-finding on the descent — the direct-looking line down cliffs out

name: Dark Glacier Route
approach: Access begins in Chelan via the Lady of the Lake passenger ferry (Lady Express ~2.5 hrs or Lady II ~4 hrs) or floatplane to the roadless village of Stehekin, then a scheduled valley shuttle bus/van up the Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge (~1,700 ft), the trailhead for the Agnes Creek Trail/PCT and the end of the road. From High Bridge there are two documented approach options to the base of the peak: (1) Traditional Swamp Creek approach -- hike the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) south about 5-5.5 miles to Fivemile Camp (2,200 ft), continuing about 3 more miles (roughly 8-9 miles total from High Bridge) to Swamp Creek Camp (2,800 ft); leave the maintained trail and follow the long-unmaintained, heavily brushed Swamp Creek climbers' path upvalley, crossing Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and pushing through roughly a quarter mile of thick slide alder and vine maple, to reach a lower basin (often not until after dark for many parties); continue cross-country from the lower basin to the upper basin (about 4-5 hours of further travel, reaching roughly 4,300 ft), then kick steps up around 3,000 ft of steep, often snow-covered terrain (no established track) to the saddle/col below the glacier. (2) Newer PCT/Hemlock Camp variant -- continue farther south on the PCT roughly 12.5 miles from High Bridge to Hemlock Camp, then leave the trail and climb northwest through open forest and slopes (about 3,500 ft of gain) directly to Dark Fin Col, avoiding most of the Swamp Creek brush; this is reported as a substantially easier approach even though it is not the route most published descriptions still describe as standard. In early May the Agnes Creek section of the PCT was cleared by trail crews only as far as 1-2 miles short of Swamp Creek camp, after which about 30 trees lay across the tread; the camp itself was snow free that month in a low-snow year.
descent: There is no separate descent route documented -- parties down-climb the same line they climbed. From the summit, reverse the short scramble to the moat, get a belay or careful downclimb across the bergschrund/moat back onto glacier ice, and descend the Dark Glacier roped as a team, staying alert for crevasses that may be less obvious on the way down and for wet, loose rock along the glacier's rock margins. Regain Dark Fin Col, then descend the approach terrain (loose/steep slopes into the basin, and either the Swamp Creek brush or the PCT/Hemlock Camp slopes) back to high camp. Given how long and strenuous the round trip from camp is, most parties plan to be back at camp well before dark and treat the final hike out to High Bridge as a separate day to make the fixed ferry/shuttle departure.
hazards: Crevasses on the Dark Glacier require roped travel and active routefinding, especially later in the season.
The Swamp Creek approach involves a log crossing of Swamp Creek and roughly a quarter mile of dense slide alder/vine maple brush.
Loose, wet rock is present below snow slabs near the glacier margins and around Dark Fin Col.
The summit moat/bergschrund crossing is exposed and typically requires a belay.
Extreme remoteness (boat/floatplane-only access, no road, no cell coverage) magnifies the consequences of any injury or delay.

waysIn.name: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
waysIn.season: Early to mid summer gives firm, well-bridged snow with least crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are open and the glacier is less stable.
waysIn.notes: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.
hazards: About a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple on an officially abandoned path
A forested cut up the headwall to the right of the waterfall looks like the way and is not — taking it forces a Class 3/4 rock wall in the trees
The slab cut onto the glacier is easy snow early in the season and a gully with a stream running in it later, needing Class 2/3 slab work
The glacier is genuinely crevassed; roped travel with crevasse rescue capability is the expectation
Wet-loose runouts come off snow slabs perched on wet rock along the glacier margins
The moat crossing onto the summit rock varies through the season and can be the hardest move of the climb late in a dry year

waysIn.name: Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
waysIn.season: Early to mid summer for the best glacier conditions, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
waysIn.notes: The newer variant continues farther south on the crest trail, roughly to the Hemlock camp, then leaves the trail and climbs northwest through open forest and slopes — about 3,500 ft of gain — to reach the glacier from the ridge above. It avoids nearly all of the Swamp Creek brush and is substantially easier ground, even though the Swamp Creek line is still the one usually called standard. It is the better choice for a party that wants to arrive with something left, and it is what the far side of the ridge separating this peak from its neighbour gives access to.
hazards: Trackless climbing through open forest and slopes with no established line
The drop-in onto the glacier off the ridge has needed a rappel
Crevasses, and the season-dependent moat crossing onto the summit rock
The gentle-looking snowfield on the north side of the summit ridge ends in a dead vertical rock face
Many unbalanced rocks on the final crest, and cornices along it early in the season
waysIn.whyThisWay: To skip the thick Swamp Creek brush on easier forest slopes, though recent beetle deadfall at the old camp and on the climb to the col slows the steep start and makes it less attractive.

name: North Face
approach: Approached through Davis Peak's northern cirque from the Stetattle Creek side, north of the peak; no detailed trailhead-to-base mileage is recorded.
hazards: Large, sometimes loose chockstones in the summit gully.
A serious, committing alpine rock route on one of the biggest, least-documented walls in the North Cascades.

name: South Slope and Ridge
approach: There is no trailhead in the usual sense — you step off the highway into the forest. Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 123, or about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge. There are parking lots at each end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles, so park at the west lot. Elevation here is 1,096 ft, and there are accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the Gorge Creek Falls viewpoint. Walk across the bridge to its east end, go a few feet farther east, cross the highway, and pick the easiest place to start uphill into the woods. That is the whole approach: the route and the approach are the same thing from here, 6,000 vertical feet of it. Round trip is about 6.2 miles with roughly 6,000 ft of gain in three miles. Carry water. The slope is south-facing and dry once the snow is gone, and there is no reliable source between the highway and the snowfields high on the mountain. In late spring, snowmelt on the route solves this and simultaneously suppresses the brush, which is why that window is the usual recommendation.
descent:
Descend the south ridge crest directly rather than reversing the east-basin variation. The step that drops into the saddle looks formidably steep from camp — steep enough that at least one party detoured around it on the way up — but it is climbed down easily, with all the ledges you need. Below the saddle, retrace your line through Point 5872 and the open slopes.

The work is in the forest. Stay on the line you came up: the cliff bands near 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft need to be turned on the correct side, and getting them wrong means rappelling off trees. Slabs low on the mountain are covered in slippery moss, and one party reported a 3rd-class chimney with an awkward move below it as the crux of the descent. Expect deadfall fields. Total descent time is about 4.1 hours from the summit for a fit party moving well, and every account calls it brutal on the knees.

If you are descending this route after climbing the northeast face, the strong advice from the party that did it is to get the top 1,500 ft done in daylight — that is what lets you avoid the cliff bands — and to carry a compass, because the timber is dense enough to hide the dam lights and a drift to the east puts you in Stetattle Creek.
hazards: Cornice collapse along the summit ridge; the crest itself is corniced and overhangs a 5,250-ft face.
Route-finding failure in the cliff-banded forest, which is the most likely cause of an epic on this route in either direction.
Heat and dehydration on a fully south-facing 6,000-ft slope in summer, with no water available.
Wet-loose avalanche and mush snow on the south aspect from midday onward in spring.
Severe cold and cornice exposure at the 5,720+ ft saddle camp in winter — one party recorded -22F.
Slippery moss-covered slabs and unstable deadfall low on the mountain.
Falls on steep snow at the 65-degree notch, where a slip has consequences.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead (~2,360 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, where the pavement ends. Walk the gated road/trail roughly 1 mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724, branching right off the old railroad grade. The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber via switchbacks, fording Weden Creek about 1 mile in (the crossing can be a wet, rock-hop affair in early season or after rain). About 1.2 miles past the creek crossing (roughly 3 miles from the trailhead), the trail crosses a steep avalanche/snow gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July — this is the trail's main hazard and can require an ice axe or careful kick-stepping in early season. Above treeline the trail breaks into subalpine meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin (~5,000 ft); tread carefully off-trail here as the meadows are fragile and use rock/gravel where possible. From the basin, follow the boot path past a small tarn and up boulder/talus slopes to Foggy Lake (~5,200 ft, about 4.7 miles from the trailhead) — the lake is a reliable water source (filter before drinking) and the last easy flat camping/staging area. From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then ascend Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward ~6,200 ft, aiming for the main summit gully. Route-finding caution: the obvious gully looks like the natural line but ends in a vertical wall — the actual route exits the gully and moves onto class 3-4 rock just left of it about 100 vertical feet below the top, working up to a notch/col at roughly 6,350 ft. From the col, turn west/left and scramble the final short pitch to the true summit (6,610-6,615 ft). Total is about 11-14 miles round trip, depending on the exact approach line, with roughly 4,200-4,300 ft of gain to the summit; snow can linger in the gully and basin into early September, and a helmet is strongly recommended for the loose upper rock. In early July the trail from about 4,000 ft is snow-covered, the basin lakes are still frozen, and soft snow persists up to the notch below the summit gully.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the class 3-4 rock left of the gully back to the ~6,350 ft col, then descend the blocky wall/rock slope back into the main gully system and down the south-facing slopes to Foggy Lake. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling required; care is needed staying on the correct (looker's-left) rock rather than drifting into the steeper, wall-capped gully proper. Some parties note a narrow gully on the bluff above Foggy Pass (west of the true pass) that offers an alternate downclimb/traverse option back toward Foggy Lake if conditions or crowding make the standard line awkward. From Foggy Lake, retrace the boulder field and boot path back through Gothic Basin, re-cross the avalanche gully and Weden Creek, and descend Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724 back to Barlow Pass. The descent through the upper talus/scree is notably slow and knee-jarring; snow lingering in the gully or basin can actually ease the descent (plunge-stepping/glissading) in early-to-mid season but adds slip hazard if icy.
hazards: steep talus and slabs
snow in the basin early season
exposure near summit

waysIn.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; the trail's snow gully can need an axe into July
waysIn.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead, about 2,360 ft, where the Mountain Loop Highway pavement ends. Walk the gated road roughly a mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin Trail #724, which branches right off the old railroad grade.

The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber, fording Weden Creek about a mile past the junction — a wet rock-hop in early season or after rain. Roughly 1.2 miles above the creek, and about three miles from the trailhead, the trail crosses a steep avalanche gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July. That crossing is the main hazard on the walk in.

Above treeline the trail breaks into the meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin around 5,000 ft. The meadows are fragile — travel on rock and gravel where possible. From the basin a boot path runs past a small tarn and up boulder and talus slopes to Foggy Lake at about 5,200 ft, roughly 4.7 miles in. The lake is the last reliable water and the last flat staging or camping ground.

From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on the climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then work up Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward the permanent snowfield below the summit walls at roughly 6,200 ft.
hazards: Steep snow tongue where the trail crosses the avalanche gully, into July
Weden Creek ford
Loose rock on the upper wall — helmet from Foggy Lake onward
Blind entry into the dead-end gully in cloud

name: North Slopes
approach: Park at the large Alpental Ski Area lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 1.4 miles/2 miles up from I-90 Exit 52, per differing trip-report odometers), elevation roughly 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead or maintained trail for Denny Mountain itself — climbers cross the base area and pick up boot-track/climber's paths under the old Armstrong Express / Sessel chairline on the mountain's north-facing slopes. Early season or in a lingering snowpack this is straightforward: hike the barren lower ski slopes for a few hundred feet of gain to snowline, then switch to crampons/axe and follow the Lower International ski run up into a small basin. From there the route continues up the steep Upper International run (a double-black-diamond pitch that holds firm snow late into the year and is the crux of the ascent in spring conditions) to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station (the Edelweiss lift was rebuilt as a new Doppelmayr triple chair, opened January 2026, replacing the original 1967 Riblet double that had earned it the old 'Edelweiss' nickname on this route). In summer/dry conditions the same line goes as a rough boot-path and talus/scree scramble through brush, small hemlocks, and huckleberry — expect neck-deep slide alder and bramble in spots, loose scree underfoot, and only intermittent pink/white/blue flagging that does not reliably mark the line; route-finding is the main hazard low on the mountain. Above the lift station, angle up the wide open ramp toward the summit horn; this transitions from scree/heather to broken rock. A fixed steel cable (a short via-ferrata-style handline) protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick rock ledge traverse just below the top. The route finishes with a short Class 2–3 scramble (some parties note a stiffer Class 3–4 move) through a narrow rock cleft to the summit block, which carries an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker. One-way distance/gain from the lot to the summit runs roughly 2.3–2.4 miles and about 2,500 ft, consistent with the ~4.7 mi (7.56 km) round-trip logged for this route; best window is late spring through mid-July after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or typically used on the standard North Slopes route. Reverse the summit cleft and cable-protected ledge back down to the top of the Edelweiss lift station (rebuilt as a new triple chair in January 2026), taking care on the down-sloping ledge traverse (it is more exposure-sensitive descending than ascending). From there, most parties drop into Edelweiss Bowl rather than exactly retracing the International runs: descend the open bowl, cross east through Midway Saddle, and finish down Debbie's Gold ski run back to the base area, glissading or boot-skiing the snow where conditions allow — this is faster than downclimbing the steep Upper International pitch and is the descent line most parties use (roughly 1.3 hours down versus 2.5–2.7 hours up). In low-snow/summer conditions without a glissade path, simply reverse the ascent line of least resistance back through the ski-slope brush and scree to the base lodge, watching for loose rock and the same route-finding ambiguity encountered on the way up. Hazards on descent are exposure on the cable ledge, potential glissade-path hazards (rocks, run-out onto talus) in Edelweiss Bowl, and loose/scree footing lower down; no technical rope work is needed on this route.
hazards: loose footing
ski-area infrastructure
brief exposed Class 2-3 step/narrow ledge at the true summit
avalanche terrain on the peak's slopes when snow-covered

waysIn.name: Alpental base area and the ski runs under the old Armstrong Express line
waysIn.season: Late spring to mid-July, after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree
waysIn.notes:
Park at the large Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road, about 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead and no maintained trail for Denny Mountain. Cross the base area and pick up boot tracks and climbers' paths on the north-facing slopes under the old Armstrong Express and Sessel chair lines.

On snow this is simple: walk the barren lower slopes a few hundred feet to snowline, put on crampons and axe, and follow the Lower International run into a small basin, then the steep Upper International run — a double-black pitch that holds firm snow late and is the crux in spring — to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station.

Dry, the same line is a rough boot path and scree scramble through slide alder, small hemlocks and huckleberry, with only intermittent flagging that does not reliably mark anything.

About 2.3 to 2.4 miles and 2,500 ft one way.
hazards: Loose footing on scree and dirt once the snow has gone
Neck-deep slide alder and bramble low on the mountain in summer, with unreliable flagging
Ski-area infrastructure on the route
A brief exposed class 2-3 step and narrow ledge at the true summit
Avalanche terrain on these slopes when snow-covered

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: Devore Peak is only reachable by a multi-day approach out of Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan — there is no road access. Drive to Fields Point Landing (or Chelan) and take the Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express passenger ferry up-lake to Stehekin (roughly a 2-4 hour boat ride depending on which boat); the National Park Service shuttle bus or a short water-taxi hop then covers the last few miles to Weaver Point Campground on the north shore, which is the trailhead (some parties instead bike or hike the road from Stehekin to High Bridge/Harlequin Bridge and pick up the Stehekin River Trail on foot). From Weaver Point (~1,160 ft), pick up the Devore Creek Trail (USFS Trail #1244). The trail switchbacks steeply — roughly 30 switchbacks over about 2 miles — up through open forest to the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary at ~2,300 ft, then settles into a steady, unrelenting climb alongside Devore Creek for another 3+ miles; this middle section sees little maintenance and can be brushy underfoot. Devore Creek is crossed/paralleled repeatedly and is the reliable water source through this stretch. At roughly 4-5 miles from Weaver Point you reach Bird Creek Camp (~4,200 ft), the last established campsite and a common bivy for a two-day itinerary. From here leave the maintained tread and follow the open-forest use path/animal trails up along Bird Creek about another mile to a higher, unofficial camp at ~5,400 ft — many parties who want a single big summit day push to this basin instead. Continue upvalley along Bird Creek through heather benches and a talus staircase into a broader open basin holding the Bird Lakes (~7,000 ft); cross Bird Creek near the northern lake (last reliable water before the summit ridge). From the lake basin, climb loose Class 2-3 talus/scree southeast to a col (~7,500 ft) on Devore's southeast ridge, passing beneath a pair of distinctive rock towers locally called "the Bottles." Expect lingering snow in this basin and on the col approach well into July, sometimes requiring an ice axe/crampons on a short ~40-degree traverse; loose rock and occasional avalanche debris are the main hazards on this upper section. From the col, the route turns west along the summit ridge/west flank — ledges and shallow gullies of variable rock quality (some solid, some "kitty-litter"-covered slab) lead through Class 3-4 scrambling with a route-finding crux threading the ledge systems below the summit block.
descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the west-ridge/west-flank ledge system back down to the 7,500 ft col, then drop into the Bird Lakes basin and follow Bird Creek back down through the 5,400 ft high camp to Bird Creek Camp and the maintained Devore Creek Trail to Weaver Point. This is fundamentally a downclimb, not a rappel-dependent descent — most of the Class 3-4 terrain is downclimbed in place. The one spot that regularly gets a rope is a short, steep ~20-ft 4th-class rock step just below the summit; there are no bolts or chains, but slung webbing rappel anchors have been found in place at the edge of the summit ridge and above the step — inspect and back up any old webbing before trusting it (carry spare cord), or downclimb it with a spot/handline. At least one party describes placing two short rappels on the descent (the summit step plus one more short step lower on the ridge where a loaded pack makes downclimbing feel insecure); a single 30m rope, or a doubled 60m rope, is more than enough length for either. Treat this as an optional-rappel route: confident scramblers downclimb the whole thing with zero rappels, while parties less comfortable with exposed 4th class commonly place one or two short raps off natural anchors. The bigger real hazard on descent is footing — the ridge and the approach basin are loose talus, scree, and "kitty-litter" over slab, and at least one climber has taken a ~15-ft scree fall here with contusions and a bruised rib, so move carefully, spread the party out to avoid rockfall onto those below, and expect the ~7,200 ft of elevation loss back to Weaver Point (and the ferry schedule back down Lake Chelan) to be a long day.
hazards: very long remote multi-day approach (boat/ferry to Stehekin, then trail and cross-country travel)
routefinding on broad ridge and open talus benches
exposed, unavoidable low-5th-class crux move on the true summit block
loose rock on the southeast face and near the summit tower

waysIn.name: Devore Creek Trail and the Bird Creek basin
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the basin and on the col approach well into July.
waysIn.notes: There is no road to this side of the valley: come up the lake by passenger ferry, then reach the Devore Creek Trail either by shuttle to the Harlequin Bridge stop and three flat miles of river trail, or by water taxi to Weaver Point and join the same junction from the other direction. The trail then climbs hard — roughly thirty switchbacks through rock bluffs to the wilderness boundary, then a relentless grade alongside Devore Creek on lightly maintained, brushy tread. Above the established camp, leave the trail and follow use paths and animal trails up along Bird Creek, gaining a hundred feet or so of hillside before sidehilling rather than fighting up the creekbed. Heather benches and a talus staircase, then a looser gully of scree and dirt, open into the lake basin near 7,000 ft.
hazards: Lightly maintained, brushy tread on the middle section of the trail
The gully out of the creek tops out in a false, larch-filled minor basin before the real lake basin
Snow on the north side of the Bottles into July, with a short stretch around forty degrees — crampons wanted
Later in the season that snow shrinks to a moat squeeze at its edge that parties have backed off
An exposed ledge traverse across the southeast face with mixed rock, some solid and some slab under loose gravel
A short vertical step below the summit with no cracks, only ledges and slabs, that most parties rappel on the way down
A false summit before the true one

name: Direct North Buttress
approach: Bear Mountain sits deep in the Chilliwack Range and is reached almost entirely on foot from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead: hike over Hannegan Pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail down-valley, then leave the maintained trail at the Bear Creek confluence and climb steep brushy timber to the meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide to a high camp on the broad saddle near 6,480 ft. From camp the Direct is reached by dropping to the glacier remnant below the wall and tying in where the toe of the buttress meets the snow; the descent from the summit returns to the same camp. The trailhead-to-camp leg is roughly 21 miles and 6,500 ft of gain, usually split over two days with a night on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek, because the camp at the Bear Creek confluence has been closed since the 2021 fire. Round trips typically run 5-6 days, about 45 miles and roughly 12,000 ft of gain.
descent: Climbers typically leave their rack and rope near the top of the technical climbing, then solo easy terrain to Bear Mountain's summit before descending snow slopes through cliff bands back toward the high camp.
hazards: loose rock in sections
remote committing position
sparse protection on some pitches
weather exposure

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
waysIn.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
waysIn.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing in high water; cable car or ford
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
Steep brushy timber, slide alder and a loose divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir below the wall
Deep moat at the toe of the buttress late season
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Remote and committing, several days from help

waysIn.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
waysIn.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
waysIn.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
hazards: International border crossing on foot
Overgrown, unmaintained tread; heavy bushwhacking on the cross-border stretch
Same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall below the buttress
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Cross-border rescue complications; remote and committing
waysIn.whyThisWay: Normally the shortest way in, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

name: Direct Southwest Buttress
approach: Shares the standard Southwest Buttress's approach and the broader Eldorado-area approach: from the Cascade River Road trailhead (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River and climb the climbers' path through forest and talus into Eldorado/Roush Creek Basin, then up to an Inspiration Glacier-area high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft (~5.8 mi, ~5,500 ft gain from the car). From camp, cross the Inspiration Glacier to the Inspiration-McAllister col, descend onto the McAllister Glacier (best passage on its skier's right side near steeper crevassed sections), and ascend the prominent gully — often snow-filled year-round — that runs from about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass up to the base of the buttress; a rope-up may be needed here as a moat guarding the base of the climb can present an exposed, deep gap. Where the Direct start diverges from the standard 1985 line: instead of traversing right partway up the approach gully/lower buttress, continue straight up ("strait up" per the route description) from the same gully entry point onto two direct-start pitches of 4th/low-5th scrambling leading to three vertical cracks; the rightmost of these is climbed at 5.8-ish through the crux to a large bench, after which an awkward 5.8+ section and blocky mid-5th rock rejoin the standard 1985 route for the remaining pitches to the summit ridge.
descent: The Direct start rejoins the standard Southwest Buttress after its first two pitches, so the descent is the same as the standard route's: from the top, return to the head of the approach gully and make a single-rope rappel (climbers may need to downclimb or work around an open moat at the bottom). Alternatively, from a large rock on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, a fixed rappel ring and sling anchor lets you make a double-rope (two-strand) rappel down to a steep snow section that still connects to rock, avoiding a direct moat crossing via a snow bridge that has historically stayed solid there. From the bottom of either rappel, descend the glacier back down to the notch/col where you left the McAllister Glacier on approach, then reverse the glacier crossing back to high camp. Because this is a mixed rock/snow/glacier descent with an in-situ ring anchor plus natural gully rappel stations, carry standard rappel backup material (a few slings/cord) in case fixed gear needs supplementing, and reassess the moat/snow-bridge crossing each trip since it is snow-condition dependent and can deteriorate later in the season.
hazards: Crevasse and moat crossings on the Eldorado, Inspiration, and McAllister Glaciers.
Long, remote approach with no easy bail once on the buttress.

waysIn.name: Same gully as the standard buttress — the difference is one turn at its top
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, when the approach glaciers are consolidated and the buttress is snow-free
waysIn.notes:
The approach is the standard Southwest Buttress's, without exception: from the Cascade River Road trailhead near 2,100 ft, cross the river, climb the climbers' path through forest and talus into Eldorado / Roush Creek Basin, and on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — about 5.8 miles and 5,500 ft from the car.

From camp, cross the Inspiration Glacier to the Inspiration-McAllister col, descend onto the McAllister Glacier (the best passage is on its skier's right side near the steeper crevassed sections), and ascend the prominent, often snow-filled gully that runs from about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass up to the base of the buttress. A rope may be wanted here: a moat guarding the base can present an exposed, deep gap.

Everything to this point is shared with the 1985 standard line. The two routes part company at the top of the gully, and after two pitches they rejoin.
hazards: Crevasse and moat crossings on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
A long, remote approach with no easy bail once you are on the buttress
Sustained 5.10 low on the route, which is the wrong place to discover the crux pitch is wet
Loose rock on the upper pitches once the two routes have rejoined

name: Direct West Face
approach: Park at the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166 (about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff heading west from Winthrop, roughly 4 miles east of Washington Pass). A climbers' boot path drops steeply off the highway shoulder through loose talus and duff and reaches Early Winters Creek at about 4,080 ft, where log crossings get you across (use caution in early-season high water). From the creek the trail firms up for roughly a quarter mile through forest before angling steeply uphill between two feeder gullies, gaining close to 2,400 ft to a flat bench at about 6,460-6,500 ft below the spires — the standard bivy/staging camp for the Wine Spires. Water here is unreliable late season; some parties find a small seasonal trickle (locally nicknamed 'Jesus Spring') in a dry sandy side-gully near the bench, but don't count on it. From the bench camp, continue up and right (east), passing a couple of minor buttresses, to gain a broad talus/scree gully that runs directly to the base of Pernod's west face — the tallest wall in the Wine Spires. The last few hundred feet of this gully are loose, ball-bearing scree over slab (cairns mark the better line); trekking poles help a lot, and helmets should go on well before entering the gully because of rockfall potential from any party above. All told it's roughly 3,000-3,500 ft of gain over about 2-2.5 miles one-way from the car to the base of the route.
descent: From the top of the Direct West Face, rappel east down the gully to the Pernod-Chablis notch (rappel 1), then make a couple more rappels down steep slabs to the neve/snowfield below (rappels 2 and 3) — three rappels total to get off the technical ground. Two 60m ropes are needed for these. The only fixed rappel anchor on the route is on the summit ridge, where nuts have been left in place; everything else, including the old aid bolts used to reach the summit block (one reported missing a hanger, another loose in its hole), should be treated as unreliable — back up or build natural gear anchors in cracks/horns where you can. From the neve, trend north around the base of Chianti Spire and climb back up to Burgundy Col (~7,770 ft), then descend the climbers' path down the scree gullies to the bench camp and boot path back to the highway pullout. Budget real time for this — the three raps only get you to the neve, after which there's a substantial re-ascent to the col before the walk-off begins.
hazards: Runout (R-rated) sections with sparse natural protection
Loose rock/rockfall potential typical of the Wine Spires' granite, especially on the approach gully
Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer
Fixed rappel anchors on Washington Pass towers can be old — inspect before weighting

waysIn.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then up and right past two minor buttresses into the talus gully under the tallest wall
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff heading west from Winthrop and roughly 4 miles east of Washington Pass. A climbers' boot path drops steeply off the highway shoulder through loose talus and duff and reaches Early Winters Creek at about 4,080 ft, where log crossings get you across; use caution in early-season high water.

From the creek the trail firms up for roughly a quarter mile through forest before angling steeply uphill between two feeder gullies, gaining close to 2,400 ft to a flat bench at about 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard bivy and staging camp for the Wine Spires. Water there is unreliable late season; some parties find a small seasonal trickle in a dry sandy side-gully near the bench, but do not count on it.

Roughly 3,000-3,500 ft of gain over about 2-2.5 miles one-way from the car to the base.
hazards: The only fixed rappel anchor on the route is on the summit ridge, where nuts have been left in place
Old aid bolts on the route, one reported missing a hanger and another loose in its hole
Ball-bearing scree over slab in the last few hundred feet of the approach gully
A descent onto the opposite side of the spire followed by a substantial re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Unreliable water at the bench camp late season

name: Dome Glacier
approach: From the Downey Creek Campground trailhead (~1,450 ft) on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), take the Downey Creek Trail #768, staying on the east bank of Downey Creek through old-growth forest. The trail is rough and lightly maintained — expect brush, downed timber, and washed-out sections; a footlog or ford may be needed at Bachelor Creek (~6.5 mi in), which has been scoured by past avalanches that swept debris across the valley and buried sections of trail. Beyond Bachelor Creek the trail climbs steeply out of the valley toward Cub Lake, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft from the trailhead; this stretch crosses open avalanche paths below Spire Point that should be assessed for stability in early-season snow. Camp is typically made in meadows southeast of Cub Lake (~5,300 ft) or, better positioned for summit day, up on the ridge above at ~6,200 ft (add ~1 hr from the lake). Reported car-to-camp time is 9-11 hours given the distance, brush, and elevation gain — budget this as a genuine multi-day approach, not a day hike-in. From high camp, a boot path crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, then the route drops ~200 ft and traverses cross-country (roughly 80° bearing) below cliff bands, over glacier-polished slabs (bare rock in late season, snow-covered early season) and a boulder/snow slope, to gain the base of the Dome Glacier. This traverse is unmarked route-finding on exposed, sometimes loose terrain — a map/compass or GPS track is strongly recommended.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the rock arête (~500 ft) back to the notch at 8,560 ft, then down the snow slope (~300 ft) onto the Dome Glacier, and back down-glacier along the ascent track to the base of the climb, retracing the cross-country traverse back to high camp. The rock arête itself is narrow, exposed, and largely featureless — many parties belay or fix a handline/rappel for at least part of it rather than downclimbing unroped, especially in the upper section near the summit. The more consequential technical step is typically the bergschrund on the Dome Glacier below the notch: depending on the season and how open the 'schrund is, parties commonly need one rappel (single 60m rope reported sufficient) to get down past it safely, building an anchor from snow pickets, a buried deadman, or a v-thread in firm ice — there are no fixed/bolted anchors on this remote, seldom-traveled route. In a low-snow year or if the bergschrund is well-bridged, this step may be downclimbable with no rappel at all, so treat the rappel as conditions-dependent rather than fixed. Below the glacier, re-cross the loose/polished traverse back toward Cub Lake camp with care, then descend the Downey Creek Trail back to the trailhead, watching again for the avalanche-debris and washout sections near Bachelor Creek.
hazards: crevasses
remoteness
brushy approach

waysIn.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
hazards: Brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log; trail destroyed by an old avalanche swath near 4,500 ft
Open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Dome Glacier
Narrow, exposed rock arete near the summit; many parties belay or rappel part of it
Cairned cross-country traverse to the glacier is easy to lose in cloud
Cornices on the upper ridge; remote, multi-day approach

waysIn.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
hazards: Multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
Crevasses on the Dome Glacier and a bergschrund below the notch
Narrow, exposed rock arete near the summit; many parties belay or rappel part of it
Cornices on the upper ridge
Remote terrain, long evacuation if injured
Camp at the Dome-Dana col has snowmelt water only
waysIn.whyThisWay: When Dome is reached as part of the whole Ptarmigan Traverse, camping at White Rock Lakes; it is much longer and needs glacier skills, so it is not chosen for Dome alone.

name: East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier
approach: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado Trailhead (~2,100 ft; first 10 miles paved, remainder rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Eldorado Trail through forest, cross a creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft (roughly 4 miles and ~6,000 ft of gain). From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the col at the base of Dorado Needle's East Ridge.
descent: From the summit, avoid old/misleading rappel tat and head toward the Northwest Ridge. Locate a wrapped-block rappel anchor a short distance above a stance; rappel roughly 30m (100 ft) to another stance, then scramble easy ledges to a further, uncomplicated rappel that lands in a moatless notch. From there, navigate steep crevasses on climber's right to regain the McAllister-Inspiration col and the glacier route back to camp.
hazards: Remote, heavily glaciated approach with real crevasse-fall potential on the Inspiration and McAllister Glaciers
Loose rock low on the route demands cautious, tested protection placements
A complex, easy-to-misroute Northwest Ridge descent with moat and rappel-anchor hazards

waysIn.name: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
waysIn.season: July through September, once glacier bridges and moats have stabilised but before the early-season storms return
waysIn.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,100 ft — the first ten miles paved, the rest rough gravel and high-clearance recommended. Hike the Eldorado climbers' trail through forest, cross the creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft, roughly four miles and 6,000 ft of gain.

From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the col between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle at about 7,600 ft. That col is the base.

Most parties take eight to twelve hours round trip from high camp, and descend by the Northwest Ridge rather than reversing this line — which means the day ends on unfamiliar ground with rappels and a moat, so scout the Northwest Ridge's top as you pass it.
hazards: Crevasse-fall potential on the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
Loose, thinly protectable rock on the first pitch off the col — test every placement
A bottomless moat on the glacier traverse partway up the route, where the line steps off the ridge and back on
A complex, easy-to-misroute Northwest Ridge descent with moat and rappel-anchor hazards at the end of a long day
